signals.title: [Serve] Fix ZeroDivisionError in router and AttributeError in Deployment.__eq__
signals.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Two boundary check bugs in Ray Serve: 1. `prefix_aware_router` crashes with `ZeroDivisionError` when `input_text` is an empty string (e.g., for unsupported multimodal content that yields no extractable text). The match rate calculation `len(matched_text) / len(input_text)` divides by zero. 2. `Deployment.__eq__()` directly accesses `other._name` without checking if `other` is a `Deployment` instance. Comparing a `Deployment` to any non-Deployment object (string, None, int) raises `AttributeError`. ## What changes are made? - `python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/routing_policies/prefix_aware/prefix_aware_router.py`: Add empty string guard before match rate division, setting `match_rate = 0.0` to trigger fallback routing - `python/ray/serve/deployment.py`: Add `isinstance(other, Deployment)` guard returning `NotImplemented` per Python's data model convention - `python/ray/llm/tests/serve/cpu/deployments/test_prefix_aware_request_router.py`: Add test for empty input handling - `python/ray/serve/tests/unit/test_schema.py`: Add tests for `__eq__` with non-Deployment types - Minor formatting adjustment in `deployment_to_schema` (parenthesized ternary, auto-formatted by black) ## Related issues Fixes #64573 Fixes #64574 ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (using `git commit -s`) - [x] I've run pre-commit hooks (ruff, black, semgrep, pydoclint) to lint the changes - [x] I've added tests for the new behavior

signals.title: [jobs] Simplify job submission failure stack traces
signals.text: ## Description When `ray job submit` fails (e.g. duplicate `submission_id`), the CLI currently lets the raw `RuntimeError` from the dashboard SDK propagate, so the user sees ~40 lines of nested tracebacks spanning the CLI, dashboard SDK, job head, job agent, and job manager forwarding chain, with the actual actionable error buried at the very bottom. This wraps the `client.submit_job(...)` call in the `submit` CLI command and extracts the innermost exception stack via a small regex helper, then reports it through the existing `cli_logger.abort(...)` (which prints the message without a Python traceback). If the expected pattern isn't found for any reason, the original message is returned unchanged, so behavior degrades safely rather than hiding information. ## Related issues Fixes #64619 ## Additional information Tested locally: - `pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/tests/test_cli.py python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/tests/test_cli_utils.py` — 36 tests pass (32 existing + 4 new unit tests for the extraction helper + 1 new CLI-level test for the simplified output). - The extraction helper was also run directly against the traceback shape from the issue, using local paths. The previous PR description reused the exact `/Users/rliaw/...` traceback from the issue without clearly saying so. That was misleading — here is the equivalent output produced from my own local checkout: **Before (raw nested traceback):** ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/.venv/bin/ray", line 8, in <module> sys.exit(main()) File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/scripts/scripts.py", line 3010, in main return cli() File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/sdk.py", line 268, in submit_job self._raise_error(r) RuntimeError: Request failed with status code 500: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/job_head.py", line 407, in submit_job resp = await job_agent_client.submit_job_internal(submit_request) File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/job_head.py", line 144, in submit_job_internal await self._raise_error(resp) RuntimeError: Request failed with status code 400: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/job_agent.py", line 45, in submit_job submission_id = await self.get_job_manager().submit_job( File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/job_manager.py", line 555, in submit_job raise ValueError( ValueError: Job with submission_id pytorch-mnist-job already exists. ``` **After (with this PR's `extract_concise_error_message`):** ``` RuntimeError: Request failed with status code 400: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/job_agent.py", line 45, in submit_job submission_id = await self.get_job_manager().submit_job( File "/home/mac/rahil/oss-contributions/ray/python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/job_manager.py", line 555, in submit_job raise ValueError( ValueError: Job with submission_id pytorch-mnist-job already exists. ``` As requested in the earlier review round, the output keeps the full last stack (the innermost `RuntimeError: Request failed with status code 400` hop plus the `ValueError: Job with submission_id ... already exists`) and only drops the outer HTTP-forwarding hops.

signals.title: [core/state] Make `ray list nodes` default output concise
signals.text: ## Motivation The default `ray list nodes` table output is hard to scan when a cluster has many nodes: a full 40+ character `node_id`, the `state_message` and `labels` columns, a nested `resources_total` dict column, and a per-row index all push the useful signal off-screen. Issue #64617 asks for a `kubectl get pods`-style concise default view, while keeping full information available via `--detail`. Example before (default, verbose): ``` ======== List: ... ======== Stats: ------------------------------ Total: 1 Table: ------------------------------ NODE_ID NODE_IP ... RESOURCES_TOTAL ... 0 057ae8704b49ce135e8f6665d66f44c6a81572f7e9d6475 10.x.x.x ... {CPU: 4.0, ...} ``` Example after (default, concise): ## Implementation Details ### Approach Introduce a per-schema table-rendering hook so that **only `NodeState`** changes its default layout. No other resource's output and no programmatic (json/yaml) output are touched. ### Changes **`python/ray/util/state/common.py`** - Added `StateSchema.format_table_output(cls, state_data, detail)` classmethod: a behavior-equivalent move of the existing table-rendering logic out of `state_cli.get_table_output` (same `yaml.dump` for dict values, same `tabulate(..., showindex=True, tablefmt="plain", floatfmt=".3f")`, same `Stats:`/`Table:` wrapper). Uses `cls.list_columns(detail)` so the correct subclass field list is picked up. - Overrode `NodeState.format_table_output`: - `detail=False` -> concise bare table. Columns in order: `NODE_ID NODE_IP IS_HEAD_NODE STATE NODE_NAME CPU GPU MEMORY OBJ_STORE`. `node_id` is trimmed to the first 8 chars + `"..."` (only when longer than 8). `CPU`/`GPU`/`MEMORY`/`OBJ_STORE` are promoted out of `resources_total` as their own columns. No `Stats:`/`Table:`/`List:` wrapper, no row index (`showindex=False`). - `detail=True` -> delegates to the base via zero-arg `super().format_table_output(...)` so `cls` stays bound to `NodeState` (calling `StateSchema.format_table_output(...)` directly would bind `cls` to the abstract base and lose the field list). Preserves full `node_id`, all columns, and the wrapper. - Added imports: `yaml`, vendored `tabulate`. **`python/ray/util/state/state_cli.py`** - `get_table_output` now delegates to `schema.format_table_output(state_data, detail)` when a schema is provided. A backward-compat fallback (original logic with `cols=[]`) is kept for `schema=None`, which previously raised `AttributeError`. ### Properties preserved - **json/yaml output is byte-identical**: `output_with_format`'s json/yaml branches are untouched; NodeState.format_table_output` only runs for the DEFAULT (table) format. - **Other resources are unaffected**: `ActorState`/`WorkerState`/`TaskState`/`ObjectState`/`PlacementGroupState`/`RuntimeEnvState`/`JobDetails` have no override and still render with the `Stats:`/`Table:` wrapper via the base class. - **humanify timing unchanged**: `output_with_format` still calls `schema.humanify(state)` before table rendering, so `resources_total["memory"]`/`["object_store_memory"]` are already human-readable `"X GiB"` strings when NodeState.format_table_output` reads them; `CPU`/`GPU` stay as raw numbers. ## Related issue Closes #64617.

signals.title: [Data] Make Progress Rendering Async
signals.text: ## Description This PR introduces AsyncExecutionProgressManagerWrapper that: - Executes all progress manager operations in a background thread using ThreadPoolExecutor - Allows the scheduling loop to continue immediately without waiting for progress updates - Monitors for stalled progress updates and logs warnings to help users diagnose terminal I/O issues - Handles graceful shutdown with configurable timeouts ## Related issues Closes #57781 ## Additional information `ray/data/_internal/progress/async_progress_wrapper.py` - Contains AsyncExecutionProgressManagerWrapper class - Implements all BaseExecutionProgressManager methods asynchronously `ray/data/_internal/progress/__init__.py` - Updated get_progress_manager() to wrap progress managers with async wrapper - Skips wrapping for NoopExecutionProgressManager and LoggingExecutionProgressManager - Wraps TqdmExecutionProgressManager and RichExecutionProgressManager `ray/data/context.py` - Added enable_async_progress_updates: bool = True field to DataContext - Allows users to disable async wrapper for debugging if needed tests to be added in `ray/data/tests/test_async_progress_wrapper.py`

signals.title: [serve] Call _is_router_running_in_separate_loop() in shutdown_async
signals.text: ## Why are these changes needed? `DeploymentHandle.shutdown_async` checks `_is_router_running_in_separate_loop` without calling it: ```python # handle.py, shutdown_async() if self._is_router_running_in_separate_loop: # missing () await asyncio.wrap_future(shutdown_future) else: await shutdown_future ``` `_is_router_running_in_separate_loop` is a **method** (defined on `_DeploymentHandleBase`), so referencing it without `()` evaluates a bound-method object, which is always truthy. `shutdown_async` therefore always takes the `asyncio.wrap_future(...)` branch. When the router runs in the **same** event loop, `self._router.shutdown()` returns an `asyncio.Future`, and `asyncio.wrap_future()` only accepts a `concurrent.futures.Future` — so it raises `TypeError` instead of awaiting the future. The synchronous `shutdown()` a few lines above already calls the method correctly (`self._is_router_running_in_separate_loop()`), as do the other call sites in the file. This just brings `shutdown_async` in line. The fix is a one-character change (add `()`), plus unit tests covering both the same-loop and separate-loop paths. ## Related issue number N/A — found by inspection. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] I've run `ruff` on the changed files. - [x] I've added unit tests that exercise both branches of the fixed check.

signals.title: [core] [rdt] Adding erroring for lineage reconstruction on RDT objects
signals.text: ## Description The goal of this PR is to throw an error for lineage reconstruction on RDT objects. In order to demonstrate this functionality, we must first define what lineage reconstruction on RDT objects means. Lineage reconstruction for object store is defined when all copies of an object are gone within the cluster, which necessitates a reconstruction of the missing object. For RDT, I believe there are two scenarios that can exist for lineage reconstruction: 1. We are reconstructing an RDT object directly. ``` class RecvActor: @ray.method(tensor_transport="DEFINED") def recv(self, obj): return obj echo _ref = send_actor.echo.remote(one_mb_tensor) ref = recv_actor.recv.remote(echo_ref) # send_actor dies ray.get(ref) ``` 2. We are reconstructing an object store object ref that was created by a task that depends on RDT. ``` class RecvActor: def recv(self, obj): return obj echo _ref = send_actor.echo.remote(one_mb_tensor) ref = recv_actor.recv.remote(echo_ref) # send_actor dies ray.get(ref) ``` NOTE: Let us assume send_actor.echo is annotated correspondingly if it is a bidirectional tensor transport. The difference is subtle, but in the case for 1, we are defining return obj as an RDT ref, while for 2 this would just be a normal object store ref. ### 1. Reconstructing RDT Object Directly For this PR, we assume the following for RDT objects. If these assumptions ever break, then this PR would need to be reevaluated: 1. RDT objects have only one primary location within the cluster. 2. On ray.get / invocation for an RDT object, a new copy is pulled EVEN IF an old copy still exists. For case 1, along with these assumptions, lineage reconstruction is defined as when the RDT object producer doesn't exist anymore anywhere in the cluster. However, this case would be covered by current RDT erroring semantics. The reason is because of the assumptions above, where we pull a new copy every invocation. This is apparent for both unidirectional + bidirectional transports, as shown in the following existing test cases: - `test_nixl_abort_sender_dies_before_sending`: NIXL fails with an error if a receiver is trying to query an object from a dead actor - `test_send_actor_dies_before_sending`: GLOO fails with an error in similar scenario ### 2. Reconstructing an Object Store ref With RDT Lineage This case is what the PR tackles for RDT objects. If we are reconstructing an object store ref that has arguments created by RDT, we will be unable to reconstruct its arguments. In current implementations, this will throw an error since the lineage tracking for RDT objects are incorrect. Running the same test on the master branch gives the following error: [2026-07-13 22:23:43,355 C 5754 8489127] reference_counter.cc:617: An unexpected system state has occurred. You have likely discovered a bug in Ray. Please report this issue at https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues and we'll work with you to fix it. Check failed: it->second.submitted_task_ref_count > 0 Thus, for RDT arguments we would want to throw an error, as described in the following implementation section. ## Implementation In this PR, we keep track of any resubmitted tasks by lineage reconstruction. If the task spec ends up containing RDT args / RDT inlined args / returns RDT, we will immediately error out. This error will then be propagated down the lineage to the original caller, which will result in an error. ## Testing 1. I included tests for ensuring `ResubmitTask` unit tests fails when RDT args / RDT inlined args / RDT return transport method is set. 2. I added the faulty python integration test defined for case 2 above. ## Related issues Closes #60446.

signals.title: [Data] Fix normalize_block_types picking the count instead of the block type
signals.text: ## Description `TableBlockAccessor.normalize_block_types(blocks, target_block_type=None)` is documented to convert the blocks to a type chosen "to minimize the amount of data conversions", i.e. the most prevalent block type among the inputs. It unpacked the sorted `(block_type, count)` tuple in the wrong order: ```python if target_block_type is None: _, target_block_type = sorted( seen_types.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True, )[0] ``` `seen_types.items()` yields `(BlockType, count)`, so this binds the integer **count** to `target_block_type`. `try_convert_block_type` then compares that integer to `BlockType.ARROW` / `BlockType.PANDAS`, never matches, and falls through to the pandas default for every block. As a result any mixed Arrow/pandas input is silently coerced to pandas regardless of which type is actually the majority, which is the opposite of the "minimize conversions" contract. Repro (before the fix): ```python import pyarrow as pa, pandas as pd from ray.data._internal.table_block import TableBlockAccessor arrow1 = pa.table({"id": [1, 2]}) arrow2 = pa.table({"id": [3, 4]}) pandas1 = pd.DataFrame({"id": [5, 6]}) out = TableBlockAccessor.normalize_block_types([arrow1, arrow2, pandas1], target_block_type=None) print([type(b).__name__ for b in out]) # -> ['DataFrame', 'DataFrame', 'DataFrame'] (Arrow is the majority; expected all Arrow) ``` ## Fix Swap the unpacking so the block type is bound and the count is discarded: ```python target_block_type, _ = sorted( seen_types.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True, )[0] ``` After the fix, an Arrow-majority list normalizes to Arrow and a pandas-majority list to pandas; an explicit `target_block_type` and the single-type short-circuit are unaffected. ## Related issues None open. The line dates back to the `ArrowBlockAccessor`/`PandasBlockAccessor` de-duplication refactor. ## Additional information Added `test_normalize_block_types_picks_majority_type` to `python/ray/data/tests/test_arrow_block.py`. It fails before this change (mixed input comes back all-pandas) and passes after, and covers both the Arrow-majority and pandas-majority cases. ## Not a duplicate Re-checked per `AGENTS.md`: ``` gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "normalize_block_types" gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "table_block" ``` This PR is the only match on `normalize_block_types`; the one other `table_block` hit (#53460, "Added distinct function") is unrelated. ## Tests run and results ``` python -m pytest python/ray/data/tests/test_arrow_block.py -k normalize_block_types ``` `test_normalize_block_types_picks_majority_type` fails on master (a mixed Arrow-majority list comes back all-pandas) and passes with this change, covering both the Arrow-majority and pandas-majority directions. `black` and `ruff` are clean on both changed files. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used in preparing this change, disclosed per `AGENTS.md`. This disclosure is being added retroactively: the PR was opened on 2026-07-14, the same day `AGENTS.md` merged, and the omission was mine.

signals.title: [Feat][Core/Auth] Enable token authentication for local clusters by default
signals.text: ## Description Enable token authentication for local clusters by default. The table below shows the resulting behavior. Remote and worker paths are unchanged. | Entry point | `RAY_AUTH_MODE` unset, token exists | `RAY_AUTH_MODE` unset, no token | `RAY_AUTH_MODE=token` | `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` | |---|---|---|---|---| | **`ray.init()`** (new local cluster, no address) | enable + **reuse** token | enable + **generate** token | enable (generate/reuse) | disabled, no warning | | **`ray start --head`** (local head) | enable + reuse token | disabled + **warn** | enable; **raises** if no token | disabled + **warn** | | **`ray.init(address=…)`** (connect to existing) | unchanged, no auto-enable; needs token if cluster requires it | unchanged | requires token, else error | disabled | | **`ray start --address=…`** (worker) | unchanged, no auto-enable | unchanged | requires token, else error | disabled | A token "exists" if any of these resolve, checked in order: 1. `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variable 2. file at `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` 3. default file `~/.ray/auth_token` ## Related issues N/A ## Additional information To enable this for all clusters in the future: - Change the default to "token" here: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/1439e47b9b136143fbc99417cb4f50a82eff72a9/src/ray/common/ray_config_def.h#L39. That is the single source of truth, and `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` stays as the opt-out. - Remove the auto-enable helper functions from this PR (`enable_token_auth_by_default`, `maybe_enable_token_auth_if_token_available`) and their call sites in `worker.py` and `scripts.py`. - Decide whether `ray start --head` should auto-generate a token instead of erroring. The worker and connect paths would then require a distributed token, which is a breaking change. - The cluster launcher, KubeRay, and autoscaler would need to distribute the token to workers automatically. Test fixtures would need to provision a token, and every client path would need to attach it. - Update `token-auth.md` and the guides that say "disabled by default".
signals.author: MortalHappiness

signals.title: [dashboard] Configurable defaults + UI dialogs for py-spy/memray profiling params
signals.text: ## Why are these changes needed? The Ray Dashboard's profiling actions — **Stack Trace** (py-spy), **CPU Flame Graph** (py-spy), and **Memory Profiling** (memray) — expose several parameters (`native`, `subprocesses`, `idle`, `leaks`, `trace_python_allocators`, `duration`, `format`) whose defaults were **hardcoded**. The only way to change one (e.g. to include native C/C++ frames in a stack trace) was to hand-edit the request URL's query string, and there was **no way for a cluster operator to change a default cluster-wide**. This came up from a user asking whether the default value of `native` can be configured — today it can't. This PR makes every profiling parameter's default configurable and gives the dashboard UI first-class controls for them. ### Backend - New `RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_*` environment variables, read on the Ray head node, let an operator set each default. Parse sites in `reporter_head` fall back to these constants only when the request omits the parameter; an **explicit query parameter still wins**, so behavior is unchanged unless an operator opts in. - `duration` and `format` are split into **CPU** and **memory** variants, because py-spy (CPU: `flamegraph`/`raw`/`speedscope`) and memray (memory: `flamegraph`/`table`) accept **different** valid format sets and different duration defaults (5s vs 10s). A single shared default would break CPU requests. `format` defaults are validated against the correct set at load time, falling back to `flamegraph` on a bad value. - **`duration` validation now returns HTTP 400, not 500.** The endpoints previously raised a bare `ValueError` for an over-long duration, which surfaced as an uncaught HTTP 500. `_query_duration` now raises `aiohttp.web.HTTPBadRequest` for a non-integer or out-of-range value. - **The accepted `duration` range is `[1, RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_MAX_DURATION_S]`**, defaulting to the 60s cap the endpoints have always enforced. Operators raise or lower it per cluster. Configured duration *defaults* are clamped into that range at load time — with a warning naming the offending env var — so a misconfigured head node can never bypass the endpoint cap. - `native` remains **Linux-only** regardless of the default (existing guard in `profile_manager`). - `/api/profiling_enabled` now also returns the configured defaults so the UI can seed its dialogs, including `maxDuration`, so the duration field validates against the real cap instead of a hardcoded one. - The valid format sets live in `ray_constants` and are now read by **both** `reporter_head` (to validate the configured default) and `profile_manager` (to validate the request), so the accepted formats are declared in exactly one place. New env vars, all documented in `profiling.md` (10 total): `RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_NATIVE_DEFAULT`, `_SUBPROCESSES_DEFAULT`, `_IDLE_DEFAULT`, `_LEAKS_DEFAULT`, `_TRACE_PYTHON_ALLOCATORS_DEFAULT`, `_CPU_DURATION_DEFAULT`, `_MEMORY_DURATION_DEFAULT`, `_CPU_FORMAT_DEFAULT`, `_MEMORY_FORMAT_DEFAULT`, `RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_MAX_DURATION_S`. ### Frontend - The **Stack Trace** and **CPU Flame Graph** buttons (worker/actor/node/job and task variants) were bare links that hardcoded `native=0`, which also **overrode** the operator's configured default. They are now parameter dialogs — the same UX as the existing Memory Profiling dialog — so users set parameters in the UI instead of editing URLs. - All three profiling dialogs render one shared `ProfilingParamsDialog` component and seed their initial values from the defaults returned by `/api/profiling_enabled`. The hardcoded `native=0` is gone; format options are profiler-correct; the duration field validates against the backend's reported `maxDuration` and disables submit with an inline error when out of range. ## Not a duplicate Searched open PRs before starting — no PR addresses this area: ``` gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "dashboard profiling native default" # No Pull Requests gh pr list --repo ray-project/ray --state open --search "RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING" # No Pull Requests ``` There is no existing mechanism for configuring dashboard profiling defaults; `RAY_DASHBOARD_ENABLE_PROFILING` only gates the feature on/off. ## Related issues <!-- Link the source issue/discussion here if one exists. --> ## Checks AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to author this change; every changed line was reviewed by the submitter. **Backend — verified locally:** ``` pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/tests/test_reporter.py \ -k "query or clamp or validated_profiling_format" -v # 30 passed pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/tests/test_reporter.py -k "profiling_enabled" -v # 1 passed pytest python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/tests/test_profile_manager.py -v # 13 passed ``` Tests in `test_reporter.py`: `test_query_flag`, `test_query_duration_valid`, `test_query_duration_invalid_raises_bad_request`, `test_clamp_profiling_duration`, `test_clamp_profiling_duration_warns_and_names_the_env_var`, `test_clamp_profiling_duration_silent_when_in_range`, `test_validated_profiling_format`, `test_validated_profiling_format_absent_uses_fallback`, `test_profiling_enabled_endpoint_returns_defaults`. These cover that out-of-range durations surface as HTTP 400 rather than a bare `ValueError`, that a misconfigured env default is clamped with a warning, and that the CPU/memory format split rejects `speedscope` for memray and `table` for py-spy. New `TestProfilingFormatValidation` in `test_profile_manager.py` asserts both profilers honor the shared format sets — every declared CPU format reaches the py-spy command, every declared memory format maps to its memray subcommand, and each profiler rejects the other's formats. It mocks out subprocess execution, so unlike the live `TestMemoryProfiling` suite it also runs on macOS. End-to-end against a live head node (`RAY_DASHBOARD_ENABLE_PROFILING=1`): ``` GET /api/profiling_enabled -> maxDuration=60, cpuDuration=5, memoryDuration=10 GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=60 -> passes validation GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=61 -> HTTP 400 "duration must be between 1 and 60 seconds, got: 61" GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=0 -> HTTP 400 GET /worker/cpu_profile?duration=abc -> HTTP 400 "duration query parameter must be an integer" RAY_DASHBOARD_PROFILING_MAX_DURATION_S=120 -> maxDuration=120 ``` **Frontend — verified locally:** ``` cd python/ray/dashboard/client ./node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json # 0 errors CI=true npx react-scripts test --testPathPattern=ProfilingLink --watchAll=false # Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total # Tests: 11 passed, 11 total ./node_modules/.bin/eslint src/common/ProfilingLink*.tsx # clean ./node_modules/.bin/prettier --check src/common/ProfilingLink*.tsx # clean ``` The frontend tests assert, among other things, that the worker Stack Trace link produces `worker/traceback?...&native=1&subprocesses=0` (reflecting a configured `native` default), that it **never emits a hardcoded `native=0`**, and that an out-of-range duration disables submit with an inline error. `pre-commit run --files <changed>` passes (ruff, black, pydoclint, docstyle, import-order, eslint, semgrep). ## Notes for reviewers - All new endpoints/parameters stay behind the existing `RAY_DASHBOARD_ENABLE_PROFILING` security gate — unchanged. - `jax_profile` is deliberately **not** migrated to the shared `_query_duration` helper. It has never enforced a duration cap, and routing it through the shared validator would newly reject durations above the cap for JAX users — a behavior change unrelated to this PR's goal. Its docstring is accurate as-is. - `ProfilingLink.tsx` keeps its own copy of the format lists for the dropdown options, since the frontend can't import the Python constants. Plumbing them through `/api/profiling_enabled` would be a reasonable follow-up.

signals.title: [Data] Deduplicate Iceberg read task state
signals.text: *I used CODEX to analyze this problem and create this PR. I've reviewed the code and tests and stand by them. This summary is written completely by a human (me) other than very light copy editing by an LLM.* The problem I ran into was that with 50000 Iceberg read tasks the driver was serializing 50000 copies of the same information as it serialized the tasks into its object store. This PR replaces those copies with an `ObjectRef` to the same information in Ray's distributed object store and the workers fetch that data when needed. This ended up being a meaningful performance gain in driver-side task construction and serialization at scale, see the benchmarking section below. In my production use case it reduced the Iceberg read-task construction and serialization from over an hour to less than one minute. CODEX generated summary follows: ----- Large Iceberg scans currently serialize the same PyIceberg scan state into every Ray `ReadTask`. On a production-shaped scan with 50,000 read tasks, that repeated metadata prevented Ray from finishing task construction, delayed autoscaling indefinitely, and projected far beyond the head node's object-store capacity. This change stores the immutable scan state once in Ray's object store. Each read task now carries only its file chunk and the shared `ObjectRef`; the worker resolves that reference before calling the existing Iceberg read implementation. Read semantics, planning, projection, filtering, and delete handling are unchanged. ## Why this is not duplicate work [ray-project/ray#49054](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/49054) fixed [ray-project/ray#49107](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/49107) by removing the datasource's `self` reference from each read closure. The replacement partial still captures table IO, full table metadata, the row filter, and the projected schema in every task. Searches of open PRs for that issue, `IcebergDatasource.get_read_tasks`, Iceberg `ObjectRef`, `table_metadata`, serialized Iceberg reads, and Iceberg object-store usage found no PR addressing that residual duplication. [ray-project/ray#61753](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/61753) touches this datasource for unrelated checkpoint filtering. ## Benchmark A controlled single-node benchmark isolated the driver-side work changed by this PR. It created a real local Iceberg table with 1,028 fields, projected 290 fields, and replicated a planned FileScanTask to produce different task counts. For each count, the benchmark constructed the ReadTasks and stored each with ray.put, matching plan_read_op.py. Object sizes were measured through get_local_object_locations. The patched totals include both the serialized ReadTasks and the single shared-state object. | Read tasks | Base object-store bytes | Patched object-store bytes | Reduction | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 100 | 30.45 MB | 12.35 MB | 59.5% | | 1,000 | 304.54 MB | 122.40 MB | 59.8% | | 5,000 | 1.523 GB | 611.52 MB | 59.8% | At 1,000 tasks, median task construction and serialization time across three runs fell from 2.55 seconds to 0.46 seconds, a 5.5x improvement. The local fixture’s shared state was 117 KB, substantially smaller than the production workload’s metadata. It therefore demonstrates the scaling behavior without reproducing the production-sized state. On the production-shaped scan, the serialized size of one read task fell from approximately 1.63 MiB to 106 KiB. The patched implementation constructed all 50,000 tasks in 50.10 seconds, submitted the reads, and allowed autoscaling to begin. The stock implementation did not finish task construction or submit a read. Iceberg planning remained approximately 100 seconds in both cases, as expected; this change targets task serialization and construction rather than file planning. ## Tests ```text .venv/bin/pytest -q python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_iceberg.py --tb=short # 55 passed PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" bazel test //python/ray/data:test_iceberg \ --test_output=errors --nocache_test_results --action_env=PATH \ --test_env=VIRTUAL_ENV="$PWD/.venv" # PASSED pre-commit run --files \ python/ray/data/_internal/datasource/iceberg_datasource.py \ python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_iceberg.py # All applicable hooks passed ``` AI assistance was used to investigate the bottleneck, prototype the change, implement the patch, and draft tests and this description. This PR is a draft pending the human submitter's line-by-line review before review is requested.

signals.title: [Data] Bound Iceberg read task memory
signals.text: *I used CODEX to analyze this problem and create this PR. I've reviewed the code and tests and stand by them. This summary is written completely by a human (me) other than very light copy editing by an LLM.* Currently `_generate_tables()` scans all files associated with the `FileScanTask`s to produce one Arrow table and then yields the results in batches. The implication is that the memory consumption is what's needed to process all FileScanTasks at once. This change processes one `FileScanTask` at a time and yields the result in batches. This reduces the memory consumption to a function of the largest requirement for any single FileScanTask. This can be a meaningful benefit at scale when multiple files are processed per Ray task. UPDATE: @abhishekverma-ray points out in a comment that this subtly changes the PyArrow field data type, with respect to width of offsets. Before, the use `to_table()` allowed for promotion to `large_string / large_list` when needed. But with this PR's use of `to_record_batches()` that needs to always happen. An alternative idea would be to keep using `to_table` but yield back results at the file level. That reduces the memory footprint relative to the current behavior, which processes all files at once, but take more memory than the current approach in this PR which is to yield back at the batch level. I will defer to the guidance of the project maintainers on what the best tradeoff is here between the memory and the breaking(?) change of the returned types. CODEX generated summary follows: ----- Ray's Iceberg reader passes every `FileScanTask` assigned to a Ray read task into one PyIceberg `ArrowScan`. PyIceberg materializes the files in its executor before Ray can consume the resulting batches, so transient worker memory scales with the number and size of files assigned to that task. In our production-shaped workload, workers OOMed before downstream processing made meaningful progress. By default, this change calls PyIceberg's public `to_record_batches()` API separately for each `FileScanTask`. That bounds the Ray task's high-water mark to one file, preserves the task-wide row limit, and casts every result to the projected Iceberg schema so blocks do not alternate between small- and large-offset Arrow types. PyIceberg still materializes a complete file before Ray receives its batches, so this is a file-level—not batch-level—memory bound. `DataContext.iceberg_config.read_file_tasks_sequentially` defaults to `True` for that bounded behavior. Setting it to `False` restores the prior `to_table(tasks=tasks)` path, including PyIceberg's within-task cross-file parallelism and shared delete-file reuse. Disable it when a task has many small files, their combined input comfortably fits in memory, and throughput matters more than the memory bound. ## Results A local six-file Iceberg benchmark scanned 12 million rows: two million rows per file with eight random `int64` columns. Peak process memory fell from 1.855 GiB to approximately 650 MiB, a 65% reduction (2.85x lower), with the same output rows and no measurable hot-cache slowdown. As an end-to-end validation, the original reader OOMed after roughly 242 completed read tasks. The bounded reader, combined with an explicit 5 GiB Ray task-memory reservation, reached 2,343 completed reads with zero failures; peak worker-node memory was 102.5/160 GiB. The local benchmark isolates this code change; the cluster result validates the reader together with separate scheduling configuration. ## Testing - `/Users/aniskodedossett/development/ray/.venv/bin/pytest -q python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_iceberg.py -k 'get_read_task or read_basic'` — 5 passed, 52 deselected - `pre-commit run --files python/ray/data/_internal/datasource/iceberg_datasource.py python/ray/data/context.py python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_iceberg.py` — passed - `git diff --check` — passed I searched open `ray-project/ray` pull requests for Iceberg memory, `read_iceberg` memory, and `ArrowScan` Iceberg changes and found no active duplicate. AI assistance was used to investigate, implement, test, benchmark, and draft this PR. The submitter must review every changed line and validate the results before requesting upstream review.

signals.title: [Train] Add NCCL RAS health callback
signals.text: ## Description This PR adds an opt-in callback that detects hanging distributed training jobs by polling NCCL's RAS (Reliability/Availability/Serviceability) subsystem. NCCL ≥ 2.24 runs a monitoring thread inside every NCCL process that forms a peer mesh tracking per-rank health and collective op-counts. By querying the `ncclras` client and diffing collective-counts between successive polls, Ray Train can automatically detect and act on hangs that would otherwise stall a job until a torch process group timeout occurs. As RAS gives a snapshot of the current NCCL state, to determine if the mismatch is a temporary issue or a permanent one, the callback polls RAS every N seconds. If a communicator is mismatched *and* makes no progress at all across multiple sequential polls, then this most likely indicates that a deadlock / wedge / hang is in progress for that communicator. Its important to note that its possible for NCCL to continue (not hang) with incorrect data depending on the nccl operation, tensor size, nccl version, etc. In these cases, users will observe the collective-count continue to increase but often with a constant mismatch. In this version of the callback, we are not detecting those issues and focusing on purely NCCL collective mismatches which cause hangs. The callback is disabled by default and enabled with `RAY_TRAIN_ENABLE_NCCL_HANG_DETECTOR=1`, as the detection heuristics still need validation against real-world hangs (spot preemptions, pipeline-parallel send/recv comms that legitimately sit skewed for long periods) before it can be considered for default-on. ### Requirements - RAS itself landed in 2.24, but the poller parses `ncclras -f json`, and the `-f` flag requires NCCL 2.28+. If the binary rejects `-f`, or isn't on PATH, the callback logs a warning once and disables itself for the rest of the run rather than retrying forever. - `ci/docker/base.gpu.Dockerfile` pins and holds `libnccl2`/`libnccl-dev` at `2.28.9-1+cuda12.9` (previously whatever the CUDA base image shipped) so `ncclras` is present and JSON-capable in GPU CI. The build fails fast if the pin doesn't stick or the client binary is missing. This affects all GPU CI images, not just Train tests. - `py-spy` (and `SYS_PTRACE` in the container) for native stack traces at hang time. When unavailable, the callback falls back to a Python-only traceback of every thread. ### How it works - `NCCLRASCallback` lives on the controller and polls `ncclras` on a worker (ras forms a mesh-network between ranks requiring that only one of the workers to be polled and receive the whole network's state). Workers are tried in turn until one returns a usable report, and the query runs on a background thread so it never blocks the controller's poll loop. - A communicator's frozen-streak only advances when the RAS report shows a collective-count mismatch, every rank in that communicator is `RUNNING`, and *no* rank advanced *any* collective since the previous poll. Any progress on any op resets that communicator's streak; streaks are tracked per communicator so each one is confirmed on its own. - A confirmed hang requires the streak to persist for `RAY_TRAIN_NCCL_RAS_CONFIRM_DURATION_S` (default 600s), converted to a consecutive-poll count using `RAY_TRAIN_NCCL_RAS_MIN_POLL_INTERVAL_S` (default 15s), 40 polls by default, to ensure that a mismatch isn't a snapshot issue. - Before confirmation there is an escalation ladder: a `WARNING` when a communicator first crosses ~60s frozen, then a periodic `WARNING` every ~120s naming every still-frozen communicator, its stalled duration, and (in `fail` mode) the time remaining until `NCCLHangError`, alongside the human-readable `ncclras -f text` report. A communicator that resumes progress after being suspected logs an explicit recovery message. - On a confirmed hang, the callback logs the `ncclras -f text` report and captures py-spy stack traces from all workers (uploaded to `<experiment_path>/nccl_ras_hang_stack_traces/` as `rank_<i>.log`), then depending on the callback mode, in "fail" a `NCCLHangError` is raised and in "observe", a detailed log message is produced but no more. `observe` is the default; set `RAY_TRAIN_NCCL_RAS_ACTION=fail` to fail the run. - `NCCLHangError` (a `WorkerGroupError` subclass, `DeveloperAPI`, exported as `ray.train.NCCLHangError`) is treated as non-retryable by the `DefaultFailurePolicy` regardless of the `max_failures` budget, since a desync hang is usually deterministic and a restart would just hang again. ### Configuration | Env var | Default | Read on | | --- | --- | --- | | `NCCL_RAS_ADDR` | `localhost:28028` | worker | | `RAY_TRAIN_ENABLE_NCCL_HANG_DETECTOR` | `0` | driver | | `RAY_TRAIN_NCCL_RAS_ACTION` | `observe` | driver | | `RAY_TRAIN_NCCL_RAS_MIN_POLL_INTERVAL_S` | `15` | driver | | `RAY_TRAIN_NCCL_RAS_CONFIRM_DURATION_S` | `600` | driver | | `RAY_TRAIN_NCCLRAS_PATH` | `ncclras` (PATH lookup) | driver | The `RAY_TRAIN_*` knobs are read once when the callback is constructed on the driver validated eagerly (invalid values raise at construction); `NCCL_RAS_ADDR` is NCCL's variable and is read on the worker at query time. ### Known limitations - **Symmetric in-collective hangs are not detected.** RAS reports collective *launch* counts, so if every rank launches the same collective and the fabric wedges mid-op, all counts match and skew is zero. - **A rank that exited early is not detected.** A communicator is only considered for detection when all of its ranks report `RUNNING`, so a `FINALIZE`/`ABORT` rank alongside frozen peers is currently skipped. This could be considered in this implementation but I believe the Ray health checker should catch this first. - `missing_ranks` (unresponsive / considered-dead peers) is parsed around but not yet used as a signal. - No metrics are emitted yet, and there is no culprit-rank attribution — `NCCLHangError.worker_failures` is empty; the RAS text report and stack traces are the only diagnostics. ### Testing - `test_nccl_ras_callback.py` — CPU unit coverage of RAS JSON parsing (including the malformed `missing_ranks[]` comma NCCL 2.28.9 emits), `NCCL_RAS_ADDR` parsing, frozen-vs- advancing classification, per-communicator streak independence, communicators appearing and disappearing between polls, poll throttling, confirm-duration → poll-count conversion, config validation, the escalation/observe messaging, and that a failed stack dump does not suppress the hang error. - `test_nccl_ras_hang_detection.py` — GPU end-to-end scenarios (`train_v2_gpu`) inducing real NCCL desyncs in a `TorchTrainer` with the detector configured for fast confirmation. Requires ≥ 2 visible GPUs and `ncclras` on PATH; the multi-communicator subset test requires 4 GPUs and skips otherwise. - `test_failure_policy.py` — added `test_nccl_hang_error_is_non_retryable`.

signals.title: [core][joblib] Add opt-in autoscaling to ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool
signals.text:
## Description Closes #31128. The Ray joblib backend uses `ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool`. Historically, that Pool eagerly created a fixed number of actors from the cluster's current CPU count. A zero-CPU head therefore could not express a larger logical concurrency target, create pending resource demand, and scale workers from zero. This PR introduces an experimental, opt-in autoscaling policy while retaining the existing Pool and joblib abstractions. Supplying any of `min_size`, `max_size`, `initial_size`, or `idle_timeout_s` enables autoscaling; `Pool()` and `Pool(processes=N)` retain fixed-pool behavior. ```python pool = Pool( min_size=0, max_size=64, initial_size=0, idle_timeout_s=60, ray_remote_args={"num_cpus": 1}, ) ``` Pool autoscaling and Ray cluster autoscaling remain separate. Pool actors retain their existing `num_cpus=0` default. Callers must explicitly request resources through `ray_remote_args` when pending actors should create cluster-autoscaler demand. The joblib backend forwards the same options: ```python register_ray() with joblib.parallel_backend( "ray", n_jobs=8, max_size=8, initial_size=0, ray_remote_args={"num_cpus": 1}, ): ... ``` `register_ray()` only registers the backend; it does not store Pool defaults. Joblib's `n_jobs` remains the concurrency ceiling, and `max_size` may lower but never raise it. `RayBackend.configure()` now constructs the Ray Pool directly instead of mutating `joblib.pool.PicklingPool.__bases__` process-wide. Joblib's local-process memmapping arguments are intentionally ignored because Ray transfers values through its object store; other Pool arguments continue to pass through. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR Parallel["joblib.Parallel"] --> Backend["RayBackend"] Backend -->|"constructs directly"| Pool["ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool"] Submitters["apply / map / imap callers"] --> Queue["batch queue"] Queue --> Operation["BatchOperation
exactly-once result binding"] Operation --> Dispatcher["single dispatcher thread"] Pool --> Dispatcher Dispatcher --> Heap["derived READY min-heap
autoscaling mode"] Dispatcher --> Slots["fixed ActorSlot table
canonical lifecycle state"] Heap -. "indexes only" .-> Slots Slots --> Actors["PoolActor processes"] Actors --> Refs["readiness / batch / termination ObjectRefs"] Refs --> Collector["ResultThread"] Collector --> Results["AsyncResult / IMapIterator / callbacks"] Actors -. "explicit resource demand" .-> Autoscaler["Ray cluster autoscaler"] Autoscaler -. "adds worker capacity" .-> Actors ``` The dispatcher is the only thread that mutates actor lifecycle and scheduling state. ObjectRef completion callbacks only set a wakeup event; if callback registration fails, the dispatcher falls back to bounded polling. `ResultThread` independently resolves task results and never mutates actor slots. `_slots` remains the single source of truth. The autoscaling READY heap is a disposable derived index containing `(ready_order, slot_index)` pairs; stale entries are validated against the canonical slot before use. Fixed pools retain completed-batch fairness and do not populate that heap, preventing an unused entry from accumulating for every completed batch. ## Actor state machine Each bounded `ActorSlot` is in exactly one of six states: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> EMPTY EMPTY --> CREATING: actor handle created CREATING --> STARTING: readiness ref submitted CREATING --> EMPTY: readiness submission fails
terminal cleanup kills actor STARTING --> READY: readiness ref succeeds STARTING --> STOPPING: demand disappears
termination ref submitted, then kill STARTING --> EMPTY: startup failure confirms actor death READY --> RUNNING: dispatch one BatchOperation RUNNING --> READY: batch ref completes RUNNING --> EMPTY: actor death is observed RUNNING --> STOPPING: maxtasksperchild retirement READY --> STOPPING: idle timeout above min_size STOPPING --> STOPPING: grace deadline
force kill once STOPPING --> EMPTY: termination ref confirms physical exit STOPPING --> EMPTY: hard deadline
fail Pool and force cleanup EMPTY --> [*]: terminal Pool cleanup ``` State invariants and transition rules: - `CREATING` closes the transaction gap between actor creation and readiness submission. Once a physical actor handle exists, it is owned by a slot and terminal cleanup can find it. - `STARTING` actors create resource demand but never receive work. - `READY` actors have no in-flight ref and are eligible for one batch. - `RUNNING` actors have exactly one tracked batch ref. - `STOPPING` actors retain their bounded slot until a termination call ref confirms physical exit. A readiness or batch ref is not accepted as exit evidence because it can complete before `ray.kill()` takes effect. - Graceful STOPPING escalates to `ray.kill()` after 30 seconds. Failure to confirm exit by 60 seconds poisons the Pool instead of blocking capacity forever. - State preconditions and field invariants raise at runtime even under `python -O`; they do not depend on removable `assert` statements. - Fixed mode preserves the eager readiness barrier and balanced batch distribution. Autoscaling mode is work-conserving and selects the oldest READY slot through the derived heap rather than sorting every slot for every batch. Startup failures before the first healthy actor wait for peer readiness, so one failed actor does not poison a startup attempt that still has viable peers. After the Pool has been healthy, replacement failures use a bounded retry budget and deadline. Ordinary task completion does not reset that budget. A local readiness-submission failure after actor creation fails closed: the `CREATING` slot is retained, no overlapping replacement is created, and terminal cleanup owns the actor. ## Pool lifecycle ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> RUNNING RUNNING --> CLOSING: close() RUNNING --> TERMINATING: terminate() RUNNING --> FAILED: unrecoverable startup / dispatcher error CLOSING --> CLOSING: dispatch accepted work
wait for every RUNNING ref CLOSING --> CLOSED: queue and pending set empty
and no RUNNING actors CLOSING --> FAILED: stop deadline or dispatcher failure TERMINATING --> TERMINATED: fail undispatched work
force-stop actors FAILED --> FAILED: retain root cause
fail pending operations exactly once CLOSED --> [*]: join waits for exit refs TERMINATED --> [*]: join waits for exit refs FAILED --> [*]: actors force-stopped ``` `close()` drops the steady-state `min_size` floor but preserves capacity required by already accepted work. Exhausting the pending queue is not sufficient to close: all dispatched `RUNNING` batches must also complete before actor termination begins. This prevents the special actor termination call from racing with an accepted batch. `terminate()` fails undispatched work with a bounded error and force-stops actors. Terminal cleanup submits a dedicated termination confirmation ref before `ray.kill()` whenever possible; `join()` waits on those refs rather than assuming an ordinary readiness or batch ref proves actor exit. A fatal internal error is retained as the Pool's terminal cause, including for a submitter racing between `_check_running()` and enqueue. Each accepted batch is represented by a `BatchOperation`. Its result sink can be bound exactly once, whether dispatch produces an ObjectRef or a local control error, preventing duplicated or silently abandoned result publication during dispatcher failure paths. ## Class and ownership relationships ```mermaid classDiagram class RayBackend { configure() effective_n_jobs() } class Pool { batch_queue ready_heap slots: ActorSlot[] actor_deletion_ids dispatcher_thread state: PoolState } class BatchOperation { func batch result_sink result_bound bind_result() } class ActorSlot { state: SlotState actor object_ref completed_batches demand retire last_used stop_started_at stop_forced } class PoolActor { __ray_ready__() run_batch() __ray_terminate__() } class AsyncResult { add_object_ref() get() wait() ready() } class IMapIterator { next() } class ResultThread { add_object_ref() finish(exact_count) cancel() } RayBackend --> Pool : constructs without global class mutation Pool "1" *-- "max_size" ActorSlot : canonical lifecycle Pool "1" *-- "0..*" BatchOperation : queues and dispatches ActorSlot "0..1" o-- PoolActor : physical actor BatchOperation --> AsyncResult : binds ObjectRef or local error AsyncResult *-- ResultThread : owns IMapIterator *-- ResultThread : owns ResultThread --> Pool : temporary keepalive ResultThread ..> PoolActor : resolves batch ObjectRefs ``` `ActorSlot` owns the complete actor lifecycle (`EMPTY`, `CREATING`, `STARTING`, `READY`, `RUNNING`, `STOPPING`) and validates state-specific invariants after transitions. Pool independently owns an explicit lifecycle (`RUNNING`, `CLOSING`, `CLOSED`, `TERMINATING`, `TERMINATED`, `FAILED`). These are separate abstraction levels: actor transitions describe bounded physical capacity, while Pool transitions describe admission and terminal behavior for the whole API. `ResultThread` owns result collection, callback invocation, and result ordering. It keeps the Pool alive only until every expected result is collected, including wait-only and callback-only use. Dropping a partially consumed `imap` cancels its otherwise unreachable collector. Dynamic iterators finish with an exact submitted-chunk count rather than trusting a potentially stale custom `__len__`. Locally generated control errors use a process-local result representation; reporting a Ray control-plane failure does not require a functioning Ray object store. User callback failures are logged without replacing the authoritative task result, and successful map callbacks receive the same submission order as `get()`. ## Compatibility and scope - Autoscaling is opt-in; actor resource requirements never change implicitly. - `Pool()` and `Pool(processes=N)` retain fixed-pool construction, eager readiness, completed-batch fairness, and crash replacement. - Joblib's `n_jobs` remains the outer concurrency limit. Ray Pool construction no longer changes Joblib's global `PicklingPool` inheritance for unrelated backends in the same process. - NumPy arrays and iterables whose reported length changes during iteration are consumed according to actual iteration termination. - This extends the existing joblib/`multiprocessing.Pool` backend rather than adding a second task backend. - `ResultThread` remains the existing per-result collection abstraction. Replacing it with a shared collector would change callback isolation and blocking semantics and is intentionally outside this autoscaling state-machine change. - The API remains experimental and the final abstraction/layering is subject to maintainer review. ## Suggested review order 1. ActorSlot transaction and exit-proof semantics: `CREATING`, `STOPPING`, deadlines, and confirmation refs. 2. Pool close/terminate/failed transitions and exactly-once `BatchOperation` convergence. 3. Autoscaling policy and READY heap: desired capacity, readiness, retry, replacement, idle reap, and fixed-pool compatibility. 4. Joblib construction and `n_jobs` limits, including removal of global `PicklingPool.__bases__` mutation. 5. Result collection, tests, and documentation. ## Validation Validation used Ray 2.52.0 runtime wheels with the PR Python sources and the repository-pinned joblib 1.2.0. Additional compatibility checks used joblib 1.5.3. - The complete non-cluster-E2E autoscaling suite passed: **70 passed, 1 deselected** in 18 minutes 28 seconds. - The zero-CPU-head `AutoscalingCluster` E2E passed independently: **1 passed, 70 deselected**. Pending one-CPU actors scaled the fake cluster from zero and all results completed in order. - After the final fixed-pool READY-heap bounded-memory change, focused real-Ray regressions for fixed-pool construction, crashed-actor replacement, and `imap` after close all passed. - State-machine fault injection covers actor construction/readiness transactions, simultaneous and mixed startup failure, callback-registration fallback, bounded retries, STOPPING escalation, physical-exit confirmation, exactly-once batch result binding, actor death, terminal dispatcher failure, and local error delivery without `ray.put`. - Real-Ray lifecycle coverage includes lazy creation, Pool garbage collection, wait-only and callback-only results, initializer and serialization failures, actor replacement, idle reap/regrow, close/terminate races, `close()` plus `join()`, ready-actor death, recycling, and concurrent driver submissions. - The close-with-backlog test captures every actor before shutdown, waits for accepted results, calls `join()`, verifies confirmation refs are exhausted, and proves each actor is dead. This replaces a previous vacuous check that collected actors only after slots had already been cleared. - Result coverage includes callback exception isolation, callback ordering, abandoned iterators, exact iterator completion, stale/custom `__len__`, empty input, and failure-atomic map submission. - Black, both Ruff hooks, pydoclint, Python AST, trailing-whitespace, end-of-file, and added-large-file checks passed for the changed Python files. The aggregate pre-commit invocation could not install Vale because the external download ended with a TLS EOF; Vale does not match these changed Python files. - `py_compile` and `git diff --check` passed. The standard Bazel target was also invoked locally. It analyzed and built, but the bare local sandbox lacked NumPy and stopped during test import; the Ray CI image supplies the Python test dependencies, so CI remains the authoritative Bazel run. ## Duplicate-work check Open issues and PRs were checked before development. #31128 is the existing request; no competing implementation was found. #64959 is a duplicate design tracker created during development. ## AI assistance and human accountability AI assistance was used to develop and test this change. - [ ] The human submitter has reviewed every changed line and can defend the final design and implementation. - [ ] The human submitter has independently confirmed the final test results before requesting maintainer review. This PR remains a draft until both items are complete.

signals.title: [Data] Avoid concatenating multi-chunk tensor columns during row takes
signals.text: ## Summary `take_table()` can select `K` rows from a multi-chunk tensor column containing `N` rows. The existing path first concatenates the complete source column and then performs the take: ```text existing: O(N × D) source copy + O(K × D) output new: O(K × D) output + bounded scratch ``` This PR gathers eligible tensor rows directly from their source chunks into the final output. The optimization is shared by PyArrow-backed Ray Data operations that use the row-take path; it is not specific to shuffle. `ShufflingBatcher` additionally reuses prepared chunk metadata across repeated takes from the same immutable buffer. ## Implementation - Support non-null, numeric, fixed-shape Ray tensor V1/V2 columns. - Map global indices to chunk-local rows and gather directly into the final output. - Cap temporary gather/index scratch at 8 MiB per subbatch. - Preserve the existing path for single chunks, narrow tensors, and unsupported or unsafe layouts. - Provide `RAY_DATA_ENABLE_CHUNKED_TENSOR_TAKE=0` as an operational fallback. ## Results | Scenario | Time | Incremental peak RSS | |---|---:|---:| | Multi-chunk `float32[1024]`, `N/K = 49` | about `11×` faster | `0.020×` baseline | | Multi-chunk `float32[3000]`, `N/K = 10` | `3.36×` faster | `0.066×` baseline | | Single-chunk control | `1.01×` | `1.000×` | The large-scale Ray Data + Ray Train validation improved epoch duration by about `4.52×`, reduced worker peak USS by `8.2%`, and reduced object-store peak usage by `13.0%`. Following review feedback, the standalone benchmark was removed from the product source tree. The exact reproducible script is archived in [Issue #64960](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/64960#issuecomment-5162329628). ## Validation ```bash python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/data/tests/unit/test_chunked_tensor_take.py \ python/ray/data/tests/unit/test_object_extension.py python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/data/tests/unit/test_chunked_tensor_take.py \ python/ray/data/tests/unit/test_transform_pyarrow.py \ python/ray/data/tests/test_batcher.py ``` After the latest review changes, the focused tensor-take and object-extension tests passed (`63 passed`). On the source-only worktree after merging the latest master, the broader unit-test selection produced `142 passed`; the remaining 11 runtime-dependent batcher tests could not start because the worktree does not contain a built `gcs_server` binary. An earlier run in the built development environment passed the full selection (`137 passed`). Relevant pre-commit hooks also passed. Related to #64960, which contains a visual walkthrough. I searched open Issues and PRs and found no overlapping implementation. AI assistance was used in preparing this change; I reviewed the changed lines and ran the tests above locally.

signals.title: [docs] Pre-bake intersphinx inventory snapshots
signals.text: ## Summary Pre-bakes the third-party intersphinx inventories so Sphinx no longer fetches ~two dozen `objects.inv` files over the network at the start of every docs build. - Commits 26 `objects.inv` snapshots under `doc/source/_intersphinx/` (~1.7 MB total). - Rewires `intersphinx_mapping` in `doc/source/conf.py` to prefer the **local snapshot**, falling back to the existing upstream URL (or the `<base_url>objects.inv` default) if a snapshot is missing. Sphinx tries inventory locations in order and stops at the first that loads, so a present snapshot means **no network fetch**, and a missing one degrades to today's remote behavior — an info message, not a `-W`-breaking warning. The human-readable target list stays intact as `_intersphinx_targets`; the mapping is derived from it. - Adds `doc/source/_intersphinx/refresh.py` to rebuild the snapshots (it reads `_intersphinx_targets` straight from `conf.py`, so it can't drift from the build config) and a `README.md` documenting the refresh mechanism. Resolves **DOC-1050** (parent epic DOC-1046, "Reduce Ray docs Sphinx/RtD build time"). Estimated impact: ~20–60s per build, plus removal of an intermittent network-flake failure mode. ### Why The build fetches every inventory up front on every run — slow, and a real source of build-time variance. Two of them (pandas, scipy) go through GitHub release-asset redirects to signed, expiring Azure blob URLs — the most fragile of the set and the most plausible cause of intermittent silent timeouts. Snapshotting moves the staleness window into our control. Cross-reference *links* still point at each project's live docs site; only *resolution* uses the local snapshot, so the URLs Sphinx emits are unchanged. ### What staleness costs, and the refresh mechanism This is the load-bearing part of the change, so it's worth being explicit about the trade. `intersphinx_cache_limit` is unset, so Sphinx's 5-day default applies today: | | Staleness bound | Upstream **adds** a symbol | Upstream **removes/renames** a symbol | |---|---|---|---| | **Today** | published builds fetch fresh; PR builds ≤5 days | new xref resolves | xref fails → **loud `-W` failure** | | **With snapshots** | until someone refreshes | new xref fails → loud `-W` failure, fix = `refresh.py` | stale snapshot still resolves → **silent dead outbound link** | The second column is fine — it's self-announcing and one command to fix. The third is the real cost: a stale snapshot keeps resolving a symbol upstream has deleted, so the build stays green while emitting a link to a page that no longer exists. Ray CI does run the `linkcheck` builder (`doc: linkcheck` in `.buildkite/doc.rayci.yml`), but it can't catch this: the step is `skip-on-premerge` with `soft_fail: true`, so it runs only after merge and never blocks, and `linkcheck_anchors = False` in `conf.py` means it checks that the target page resolves, not the `#anchor` a symbol-level cross-reference points at. Most targets resolve against upstream's *moving* docs, so their inventory changes when the upstream project *releases*, independently of anything Ray pins — there is no Ray-side event to refresh against, which is why it has to be a clock rather than a ride-along with Ray's dependency bumps. Four targets are exceptions that set an explicit inventory URL: `pandas` and `scipy` read frozen `object-mirror-*` release assets under `ray-project`, `torch` is pinned to `docs/2.7/` while its links point at `docs/stable/`, and `tensorflow` reads a third-party GPflow mirror tracking its own `master`. For the three frozen ones a refresh is a no-op and committing a snapshot changes nothing about their staleness. All pre-existing `conf.py` behavior, unchanged here. How fast does this actually drift? Re-running `refresh.py` six days after the initial capture changed **4 of 26** — `grpc` 1.82.0 → 1.83.0 (a real minor release), plus content changes in `pydantic`, `python` 3.14, and `transformers` `main`. That rate is the argument for a scheduled refresh in one line. The mechanism, therefore: **a scheduled monthly job runs `refresh.py` and opens a PR when any snapshot drifted.** That bounds staleness at ~1 month, and it restores the loud failure — once the fresh inventory drops a removed symbol, the stale cross-reference fails on the *refresh PR's* `-W` build. That is why a refresh must land as a reviewed PR and must never be auto-merged: that build is the entire safety net for the silent case. That job is **[anyscale/docs#2441](https://github.com/anyscale/docs/pull/2441)** — a GitHub Actions workflow modeled on the existing `bump-ray-template-pins.yml`, which already refreshes Ray's docs template pins the same way. It reuses that workflow's fork and PAT, so it opens its PR from a fork and **needs no changes to this repo and no new permissions here**. It commits only `doc/source/_intersphinx/*.inv` (a guard fails the run otherwise), signs off with DCO, and reuses one `auto-refresh-intersphinx-snapshots` branch so monthly runs can't stack up PRs. > **Merge order:** land this PR first, then [anyscale/docs#2441](https://github.com/anyscale/docs/pull/2441). The workflow errors out by design if `doc/source/_intersphinx/refresh.py` isn't on `master` yet, so merging it early just produces one noisy failed run. `README.md` and `refresh.py` describe that job as the mechanism, so #2441 should not be left indefinitely unmerged either. ### Refreshing by hand ```bash python doc/source/_intersphinx/refresh.py # refresh all python doc/source/_intersphinx/refresh.py numpy torch # refresh a subset ``` Needed after adding a target, or when a cross-reference to a symbol that does exist upstream stops resolving. ### Also included `doc/.claude/skills/sphinx-fix/rules.yaml` — two rules gave advice this change invalidates: - `intersphinx-inventory-unreachable` said to re-run the build first, as a transient network blip. With snapshots committed, reaching `failed to reach any of the inventories` means **both** locations failed: the snapshot is missing or unreadable *and* the network fetch failed. A green re-run then just means the network came back while the missing snapshot is still missing, so a missing snapshot is now the first thing to check. - `py-xref-target-not-found` now notes that a third-party target which *does* exist upstream points at a stale snapshot — fix by refreshing, not by editing the reference. ### Not a duplicate Checked open PRs for `intersphinx` / `objects.inv` / `_intersphinx`: nothing in flight touches inventory pre-baking. (#60886 is a dependabot `nbconvert` bump; #64944 is the Sphinx 9.1 upgrade, which mentions `objects.inv` only incidentally and does not change the mapping.) ### Testing - `python -m py_compile doc/source/conf.py` — passes under Python 3.11 (Sphinx 8.2.3, current) and 3.12 (Sphinx 9.1.0, the in-progress upgrade target). - Offline verification driving Sphinx's own inventory loader (`_fetch_inventory_group`) with the network fetch path monkeypatched to raise: **all 26 inventories resolve from local files, 0 network calls, 157,320 cross-reference targets** — identical on Sphinx 8.2.3 and 9.1.0. (9.1's new `cache_dir` arg only affects remote fetches, so local-first is unchanged.) - `refresh.py` successfully re-fetches all 26 inventories, including the pandas/scipy GitHub-redirect mirrors. Re-run immediately before requesting review so the snapshots don't land stale: 26/26 succeeded, 4 drifted, all 26 verified as valid v2 inventories afterwards (`# Sphinx inventory version` banner present, upstream project/version parsed from each header). - `python sphinx_fix.py --selftest` → `SELFTEST OK (16 fixtures, 15 rules, 4 suppressions)` after regenerating the three affected goldens. The rule IDs, tiers, safety levels and unclassified count are unchanged; only the fix text moved. - `rules.yaml` parses under real PyYAML (the `check-yaml` hook's parser) as well as the skill's built-in fallback parser. - Read the Docs `-W` build: **green** on the first two commits; rebuilding on the snapshot refresh. I have not run the full local docs HTML build; the RtD `-W` build on this PR is the end-to-end check. ### Repo size The snapshots add ~1.62 MiB, and each refresh adds new blobs for whichever files changed. `.inv` files are already zlib-compressed so delta compression barely helps. On the observed drift rate that's roughly 0.5–1.5 MiB per refresh — call it 6–18 MiB/year — permanently, against ~20–60s saved on every build plus the removal of a flake class. Worth stating explicitly rather than leaving to be discovered. ### AI assistance This PR was prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code). I have reviewed the change line by line and can defend it end-to-end; the commands run and their results are listed under Testing above. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: [Serve][LLM] Pass remote URI as model for streaming load formats
signals.text: ## Description For streaming load formats (like `runai_streamer`), the RunAI streamer reads model weights directly from the remote object store into GPU memory, so vLLM must receive the object-store URI as its `model`. Currently `VLLMEngineConfig.from_llm_config` routes any remote string `model_source` into the download-mirror path: ```python if is_remote_path(model_source): # s3://, gs://, abfss://, azure:// hf_model_id = llm_config.model_id mirror_config = CloudMirrorConfig(bucket_uri=model_source) ``` vLLM is then handed model_id, but never the URI. Under a streaming load format the per-node download mode is NONE , so nothing is downloaded either. The engine can neither stream (no URI) nor load locally, and startup fails: `RuntimeError: Failed to create vLLM engine config: gpt-oss-120b is not a local folder and is not a valid model identifier listed on 'https://huggingface.co/models'` ## Related PRs Runai_streamer from a remote object store is broken for every remote string model_source — s3:// , gs:// , abfss:// , azure:// . The one exception, az:// , only works by coincidence: it is missing from is_remote_path , so it skips the broken mirror branch and falls through to the pass-through path. The correct fix would be to include this and https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65120 to add az:// to the scheme so it follows the logic correctly and is supported. ## Fix Make the decision inclusive of the load_format: - streaming load formats: pass the remote URI through as model instead of mirroring it. - Non-streaming formats: keep the existing mirror/download behavior, which preserves the clean HF cache-directory naming from #64110. This is the same approach Ray Data already uses (it keeps the remote model_source as the vLLM model for streaming), so it also makes the Serve and batch paths consistent. ##Testing • Added test_streaming_remote_model_source_passes_uri_as_model in python/ray/llm/tests/serve/cpu/configs/test_models.py . • Validated from_llm_config in a built ray-llm environment (Ray + vLLM) across s3:// , gs:// , azure:// , and az:// : • With the fix: all four schemes pass the URI through as model with no mirror config when load_format=runai_streamer . • Without the fix: s3:// / gs:// / azure:// fall back to model_id with a mirror config; az:// is unaffected until the follow-up https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65120 is included. • Non-streaming remote sources still mirror/download as before. pytest python/ray/llm/tests/serve/cpu/configs/test_models.py -k streaming_remote_model_source

signals.title: [core][dashboard] Return 4xx from node and actor detail APIs
signals.text: ## Description Makes three node/actor dashboard endpoints report client errors with 4xx status codes instead of 200/500. [#51417](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/51417) added the `HTTPStatusCode` enum and the `rest_response(status_code=...)` plumbing, but adoption stalled after one endpoint. Across non-test dashboard source there are currently 28 `OK` and 13 `INTERNAL_ERROR` usages versus only 4 non-500 error codes, all confined to `state_head.py` / `state_api_utils.py`. Backend (`python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/node_head.py`): - `GET /nodes/{node_id}` returned **200 with a near-empty payload** for an unknown node ID, because `DataOrganizer.get_node_info` falls back to `.get(node_id, {})`. Now returns **404**. - `GET /logical/actors/{actor_id}` returned **200 with `detail: null`** for an unknown actor ID, because `get_actor_infos` maps unknown IDs to `None`. Now returns **404**. - `GET /nodes` with an unsupported `view` returned **500**. An unsupported query parameter is a client error, so it now returns **400**. ## Related issues Related to [#51442](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51442) (umbrella: revisit Ray dashboard API status codes). Since that issue is an umbrella, this PR covers `node_head.py` only, so each module can be reviewed independently. ## Additional information ### Frontend change is required, not incidental The node and actor detail pages surfaced these cases by reading `result === false` out of the **200 response body**. axios rejects on 4xx, so those branches go dead the moment the status code changes, and the pages would sit on "Loading the node infos..." indefinitely with `msg` never updated. The SWR fetchers in `useNodeDetail.ts` and `useActorDetail.ts` now catch the 404 and set the same message they set before, preserving existing UI behavior. Consumers of `useFetchActor` (the Serve pages) already use optional chaining on the result, so returning `undefined` there is unchanged behavior. ### Tests Added `test_node_api_status_codes` (single cluster, looping over all three error paths plus the three success paths — not parametrized, since `ray_start_with_dashboard` starts a fresh cluster per invocation) and `test_actor_not_found_status_code`. Test environment: because Ray's core is compiled, these were run against the Ray Windows nightly wheel built from `3fb63d965f` — the exact base commit of this branch — with the patched `node_head.py` overlaid, so the patch was the only delta. ``` pytest -v python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_node.py -k test_node_api_status_codes 6 passed in 122.16s pytest -v python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_actor.py -k test_actor_not_found_status_code 1 passed in 19.74s pytest -q python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_actor.py 5 passed in 142.51s pytest -q python/ray/dashboard/modules/node/tests/test_node.py 7 passed, 4 skipped, 2 failed in 286.73s ``` The two failures in the full `test_node.py` run are `test_node_info` and `test_worker_pids_reported`. Both **fail identically against unpatched `node_head.py`** and are pre-existing Windows-environment issues, not regressions: worker cmdlines don't match `"ray::Actor"` on Windows, and runtime_env's uv virtualenv setup hits `WinError 206` (path length). Control run confirming the new tests are not vacuous — against unpatched code: - `/nodes/{unknown}` → `assert 200 == 404` (fails) - `/nodes?view=unknown_view` → `assert 500 == 400` (fails) - `/nodes` → `assert 500 == 400` (fails) - the three success paths → still pass - actor test → `assert 200 == 404`, body `{"result": true, "msg": "Actor details fetched.", "data": {"detail": null}}` (fails) Frontend checks: ``` npx tsc --noEmit # clean, exit 0 npx eslint # clean npx prettier -c # clean ``` Python lint: `ruff check` clean; `black` leaves the changed files unmodified. Caveats worth reviewer attention: all of the above ran on Windows rather than Ray's Linux CI, and against a nightly wheel plus overlaid file rather than a from-source build. Linux CI remains the authoritative check. ### Not a duplicate No open PR references [#51442](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51442), and the issue timeline has no cross-referenced PRs. The issue has been assigned since 2025-03-18 with no linked work; I commented on it before starting ([comment](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51442#issuecomment-5084257594)). ### AI assistance AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to produce this change.

signals.title: [Data] Better estimate decoded Iceberg read size
signals.text: _I used CODEX to create this PR, and I stand by it. This summary is mine._ Previously, Iceberg read planning used the raw total file size as its in-memory size estimate. For Parquet data, this change estimates decoded in-memory size using Ray's standard 5× encoding ratio. When complete projected-column metrics are available in the Iceberg manifest, it applies that ratio only to the projected columns; otherwise it uses a 5× whole-file estimate. Consequently, unprojected Parquet reads now estimate 5× the encoded file size rather than 1×. Since this data is present in the Iceberg manifests there are no additional file operations required for this, such as opening file footers. So planning accuracy improves with no material cost. Codex summary follows: ----- ### Summary - Use complete Iceberg `column_sizes` metrics for projected top-level Parquet fields. - Apply Ray's existing Parquet decode-ratio estimate to the selected encoded bytes. - Fall back to a 5× whole-file estimate when projected metrics are incomplete or unavailable. - Preserve non-Parquet behavior and report an empty projection as zero bytes. - Use the same estimate for datasource sizing and `ReadTask` metadata. ### Testing - `bazel test //python/ray/data:test_iceberg` — passed. - Focused estimator tests in `test_iceberg.py` — 8 passed, 54 deselected. - File-scoped pre-commit hooks — passed. - `git diff --check origin/master...HEAD` — passed. AI assistance was used for investigation, implementation, testing, and drafting this description. This upstream PR is a draft for human line-by-line review before requesting review. ### Duplicate-work check No open `ray-project/ray` issue or PR was found for projection-aware Iceberg decoded-size estimation. Searches for Iceberg decoded-size estimation, `column_sizes`, and Iceberg memory estimation returned no overlapping work.
