signal.title: [serve] Call _is_router_running_in_separate_loop() in shutdown_async
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? `DeploymentHandle.shutdown_async` checks `_is_router_running_in_separate_loop` without calling it: ```python # handle.py, shutdown_async() if self._is_router_running_in_separate_loop: # missing () await asyncio.wrap_future(shutdown_future) else: await shutdown_future ``` `_is_router_running_in_separate_loop` is a **method** (defined on `_DeploymentHandleBase`), so referencing it without `()` evaluates a bound-method object, which is always truthy. `shutdown_async` therefore always takes the `asyncio.wrap_future(...)` branch. When the router runs in the **same** event loop, `self._router.shutdown()` returns an `asyncio.Future`, and `asyncio.wrap_future()` only accepts a `concurrent.futures.Future` — so it raises `TypeError` instead of awaiting the future. The synchronous `shutdown()` a few lines above already calls the method correctly (`self._is_router_running_in_separate_loop()`), as do the other call sites in the file. This just brings `shutdown_async` in line. The fix is a one-character change (add `()`), plus unit tests covering both the same-loop and separate-loop paths. ## Related issue number N/A — found by inspection. ## Checks - [x] I've signed off every commit (DCO). - [x] I've run `ruff` on the changed files. - [x] I've added unit tests that exercise both branches of the fixed check.
signal.author: HrushiYadav

signal.title: [serve] Add max_request_retries to bound router retry loops
signal.text: ## Description The router's `while True` retry loop in `route_and_send_request` and `_pick_and_reserve_replica` retries indefinitely when replicas reject requests. `max_queued_requests` is only checked once at the entry gate, not during retries. Under sustained load with large payloads (~50MB), requests pile up in the retry loop causing OOM -- `num_queued_requests` can reach 119 when `max_queued_requests=20`. This PR adds `max_request_retries` to `RequestRouterConfig`: - Default `-1` (unlimited) preserves backwards compatibility - When set to a non-negative integer, the router raises `BackPressureError` (503) after exhausting retries - Both `route_and_send_request` (replica rejection retry) and `_pick_and_reserve_replica` (capacity queue retry) are bounded - Configurable via `RequestRouterConfig(max_request_retries=N)` or env var `RAY_SERVE_ROUTER_MAX_REQUEST_RETRIES` ## Related issues Fixes #61017 ## Additional information **Files changed:** - `constants.py` -- new `RAY_SERVE_ROUTER_MAX_REQUEST_RETRIES` env var (follows existing backoff env var pattern) - `config.py` -- new `max_request_retries` field on `RequestRouterConfig` with validator, `__eq__`, `__hash__` - `router.py` -- `_check_retry_limit()` helper, retry counter in both loops - `test_backpressure.py` -- config validation test + integration test with `max_request_retries=3` **Semantics:** - `max_request_retries=-1`: unlimited (default, no behavior change) - `max_request_retries=0`: no retries (fail on first rejection) - `max_request_retries=N`: retry up to N times, then 503

signal.text: Adds the map/reduce task bodies (`external_shuffle_tasks.py`) and the two operators that drive them (`ExternalHashShuffleMapOp`, `ExternalHashShuffleReduceOp`), on top of the runtime library from #64828. There is no user-visible change; the `use_external_hash_shuffle` flag and planner routing land in [3/3]. ## description - **Map task**: partitions its rows, writes one Arrow-IPC file per mapper (all partitions), returns one small handle (path + per-partition offset index + fetch endpoint + auth token). Bulk data stays on local disk, never enters the object store. - **Reduce task**: fetches only its partition's byte-ranges from each node's `ShuffleFileServer` over Arrow Flight, decodes, applies `reduce_fn`. - **Map op**: one map task per input group; at finish emits one lightweight wrapper per partition, all sharing a single handle-list ref plus a `__partition__<pid>` sentinel. - **Reduce op**: one wrapper in, one reduce task out. ## testing Operator-direct smoke test (`test_hash_shuffle_external_smoke.py`) runs the full map→reduce path without the planner.

signal.title: [core] Unify executor threads when enabling/disabling concurrency_groups
signal.text: ### Description Currently, the main thread is used for system-critical events like dispatching task submission. It is also used for default task execution, as long as concurrency_groups isn't defined. If concurrency_groups is defined, we create a separate executor thread for task execution on the default concurrency group, to avoid blocking task submission to background threads on a task running on the main thread. Ideally, we would use the same codepath no matter whether concurrency_groups is defined or not. ### Use case List of some requirements compiled from various user issues: - Tasks in different concurrency groups should not be blocked from dispatch by each other - Solution: Move control plane logic for task dispatch from main thread to background io event loop - All Python `threading` operations should act as expected, per concurrency group - Ex: threading.Local state should persist across tasks on the same concurrency group. - No crashes during shutdown. - User should be able to run tasks on the main thread - Ex: A non-constructor actor task should be able to install a signal handler - If the default concurrency group has 1 thread, then tasks on the default concurrency group should always run on the main thread - If the user specifies concurrency groups or max_concurrency, there should be a way to specify that a particular task needs to run on the main thread. - Be able to dynamically add a concurrency group - Ex: Needed for the “_ray_system” concurrency group, which handles background operations in Python - Get rid of boost::fiber and all the related hackery (infinitely increasing the python stack frame limit). - There shouldn’t be any surprising behavior when users incrementally update code (for example, add another CG or add an async def method). - For example, currently in Ray, I add one asyncio method and now some other method code breaks because it no longer runs on the main thread.

signal.title: [Data] AutoscalingCoordinator._reallocate_resources is O(R·N²) and holds its lock, starving concurrent datasets at scale (op_budget→0)
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen On a large autoscaling cluster (~840 nodes) running several concurrent Ray Data datasets with the V2 cluster autoscaler (RAY_DATA_CLUSTER_AUTOSCALER=V2, the default), datasets get op_budget=0 and stall — every map op shows Tasks: N [backpressured:tasks(ResourceBudget)], throughput collapses — while the cluster has resources. Driver logs repeat: ``` WARNING default_autoscaling_coordinator.py:134 -- Failed to get allocated resources for data-dataset_XXX_0. (consecutive failures: N) Returning cached value. ray.exceptions.GetTimeoutError: Get timed out: some object(s) not ready. ``` ### Root cause (py-spy confirmed, Ray 2.54.1) The cluster-singleton AutoscalingCoordinator actor is single-threaded, and _reallocate_resources runs an O(R·N²) triple loop while holding the only self._lock, blocking client get_allocated_resources/request_resources until they time out. Two compounding facts: 1. The request is one bundle per cluster node. DefaultClusterAutoscalerV2.try_trigger_scaling builds active_bundles from _get_node_resource_spec_and_count() (= ray.nodes(), one bundle per alive node). cap_resource_request_to_limits() always includes all active bundles and only caps the pending/scale-up bundles to resource_limits. So the request length B ≈ N (node count), independent of the dataset's concurrency or resource_limits. 2. _reallocate_resources is for R requesters: for B≈N bundles: for N nodes: _maybe_subtract_resources (+ a full copy.deepcopy of all node resources, recomputed from scratch). Under over-subscription the inner node loop rarely breaks early (nodes exhausted) → ~R·N² iterations. Measured (pure Python, R=7): single _reallocate_resources ≈ 1.8s at N=836 (B=150→0.21s, 600→1.27s, 836→1.82s; linear in B≈N). It's invoked on every request_resources (the request changes each cycle since it's rebuilt from live ray.nodes()), every cancel_request, and every 20s tick — no coalescing. With ~7 datasets refreshing ~every 10s, reallocations run back-to-back (≈0.7/s × 1.8s ⇒ a single core saturated). py-spy record (20s) shows 96% of coordinator CPU in _reallocate_resources/_maybe_subtract_resources (the autoscaler SDK call is ~3%). A concurrent get_allocated_resources sits blocked on self._lock, hits GetTimeoutError, and the client falls back to a cached/empty allocation → ResourceManager.global_limits = min(resource_limits, 0) = 0 → op_budget 0 → backpressure. This scales with cluster size N, not job count: because B≈N and the loop is N², even 2–3 concurrent datasets can saturate the coordinator on a large cluster. resource_limits does not mitigate it (the cap doesn't shrink the per-node active bundles). ### Versions / Dependencies Ray 2.54.1; RAY_DATA_CLUSTER_AUTOSCALER=V2 (default). ### Reproduction script - At scale: ≥7 concurrent datasets over-subscribing a ~840-node cluster → all hit GetTimeoutError + op_budget=0. - Offline (no cluster): _AutoscalingCoordinatorActor deps are injectable — construct with get_cluster_nodes returning N≈836 fake nodes, register R requesters (request_remaining=True), and time _reallocate_resources() → ~1.8s at N=836, R=7. (Standalone script available.) ### Issue Severity None

signal.title: [Data/Autoscaler] Proposal: Release all resources of an upstream op at once when it finishes, instead of step-wise scale down
signal.text: ### Description In the current Ray Data / autoscaler behavior, when an upstream operator (op) finishes processing, its resources are scaled down gradually step-by-step. This makes the scale-down process very slow, and as a result, downstream ops struggle to quickly acquire resources to process data, leading to pipeline stalls and underutilization. ### Problem - Upstream op scale-down is very slow (step-wise). - Downstream ops wait a long time before they can get enough resources. - Overall pipeline throughput suffers because of this delayed resource handoff. ### Proposal Once an op has fully finished processing its data, release **all** resources occupied by that op in a single shot, instead of scaling them down incrementally per step. This would: - Allow downstream ops to immediately claim freed resources. - Reduce end-to-end latency of the pipeline. - Simplify the resource handoff logic between ops. ### Question Is there a specific reason the current design prefers step-wise scale-down over one-shot release after an op completes? Would the community be open to changing this behavior (or making it configurable)? ### Use case _No response_

signal.title: [Ray Data]: Support TRL trainers with Ray dataset
signal.text: ### Description Ray dataset isn't compatible with TRL trainer out-of-the-box, issues found are: * Ray `prepare_trainer` ([source](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/096da0ce8aa0d24942a002edba6c7cf9d07c9492/python/ray/train/huggingface/transformers/_transformers_utils.py#L103)) overrides the HF trainer’s `get_train_dataloader` with a Ray-aware version that detects `_IterableFromIterator` and skips HF Trainer’s default sampler-creation path. This is necessary because HF `get_train_dataloader` will otherwise re-shard via `DistributedSampler` or `IterableDatasetShard`, double-sharding the data in a distributed training setup. * TRL’s trainer calls `_prepare_dataset` ([source](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/blob/23201dd7989ddde855de28a2c1d4523c06aa9d7a/trl/trainer/sft_trainer.py#L1376)) during construction, before the user has a chance to call `prepare_trainer` override. The TRL _prepare_dataset expects a `datasets.Dataset` or `datasets.IterableDataset` and calls `dataset.map(...)` for chat-template + tokenization, which will crash if the dataset is a Ray `_IterableFromIterator` as mentioned above (no `.map`, no `.column_names`) * With above, if we use Ray `prepare_trainer` and creates `_IterableFromIterator` , it crashes in TRL trainer; if we use TRL trainer's default `get_train_dataloader`, it has a double sharding issue which creates incorrect data shards and affects training quality. This is harder to detect as it doesn’t fail anything. https://discuss.ray.io/t/error-with-column-names-when-using-ray-with-trls-sft-trainer/23404/4 ### Use case Fine-tuning and / or reinforcement learning using TRL trainers and Ray datasets

signal.title: [Data] Dead Actor occupies actor pool slots which severely effects resource usage
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen ### What happened Using `ray.data.map_batches` with `compute=ActorPoolStrategy(size=1)` and `DataContext.max_errored_blocks = -1`, if the actor process exits mid-pipeline (e.g. `sys.exit(0)` from inside the UDF), the pipeline **silently hangs forever**: - The dead actor is removed from the alive-actor scheduling heap, so no new tasks are dispatched to it. - Because `max_errored_blocks = -1`, the failed block is ignored instead of aborting the job. - The pool with `min_size == max_size == 1` is **not replaced**: the dead actor entry stays in `_running_actors`, no new actor is created, and the input queue never drains. - Result: 0 schedulable actors, queued blocks stuck > 0, no exception raised, `materialize()` blocks indefinitely. My job runs on large high-efficiency cluster with huge number of spot-instances. I neede to tolerate random node failure and maintain CPU/GPU util at the same time. Those "Zombie Actors" wasted my cores. ### Versions - Ray: 2.55 (latest) - Python: 3.12.6 - OS: Linux ### Reproduction ```python from typing import Dict, List import ray class EchoPredictor: def __init__(self): self.counter = 0 def __call__(self, batch: Dict[str, List[int]]) -> Dict[str, List[int]]: import time import sys time.sleep(0.01) batch["output"] = [x * 2 for x in batch["data"]] self.counter += 1 if self.counter == 3: sys.exit(0) return batch from ray.data import DataContext ctx = DataContext.get_current() ctx.max_errored_blocks = -1 ds = ( ray.data.from_items([{"data": i} for i in range(3200)]) .map_batches( EchoPredictor, batch_size=1, compute=ray.data.ActorPoolStrategy(size=1), ) ).materialize() ``` ### Expected behavior Dead actor (zombie actor) should be released from actor pool so that new healthy actor could be created. ### Where the issue seems to originate In `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/actor_pool_map_operator.py`: - `_ActorPool.refresh_actor_state` correctly detects the actor as `DEAD` and `_update_rank` removes it from `_alive_actors_to_in_flight_tasks_heap`. - However, `_release_running_actor` is **not** called on `DEAD`; the entry stays in `_running_actors` so the pool's view of "running" is stale. - For a fixed-size pool (`min_size == max_size`), the autoscaler does not scale up to replace dead actors. - Combined with `max_errored_blocks=-1` (which makes `StreamingExecutor` ignore block failures), this leaves the pipeline in an unrecoverable, silent state. ### Are you willing to submit a PR? - [x ] Yes ### Versions / Dependencies - Ray: 2.55 (latest) - Python: 3.12.6 - OS: Linux ### Issue Severity Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.
signal.author: zhangsikai123

signal.title: [Data] ray.data.from_tf() fails on TensorFlow datasets with ragged tensors
signal.text: ### Description ### What happened + What you expected to happen `ray.data.from_tf()` currently materializes the input dataset through `list(dataset.as_numpy_iterator())`. This works for dense tensors, but it fails when the TensorFlow dataset contains `tf.RaggedTensor` values, because `as_numpy_iterator()` does not support ragged tensors. As a result, `ray.data.from_tf()` cannot ingest valid TensorFlow datasets that contain ragged data. I expected `ray.data.from_tf()` to support ragged tensor inputs and return a Ray Dataset instead of raising during conversion. ### Reproduction script ```python import tensorflow as tf import ray ray.init() tf_dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensors( tf.ragged.constant([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]]) ).concatenate( tf.data.Dataset.from_tensors( tf.ragged.constant([[6], [7, 8]]) ) ) ds = ray.data.from_tf(tf_dataset) print(ds.take_all()) ### Use case _No response_

signal.title: [Train] Step Count Discrepancy in Ray Train + TensorFlow with MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen When using TensorflowTrainer with MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy and a pre-sharded Ray Dataset (via train.get_dataset_shard() + prepare_dataset_shard()), the number of steps per epoch reported by model.fit() appears to be double the expected value. Minimal Reproducible Example: ``` import ray import tensorflow as tf from ray import train from ray.train import ScalingConfig, RunConfig from ray.train.tensorflow import TensorflowTrainer from ray.train.tensorflow.keras import ReportCheckpointCallback def build_model() -> tf.keras.Model: model = tf.keras.Sequential([ tf.keras.layers.InputLayer(input_shape=()), tf.keras.layers.Flatten(), tf.keras.layers.Dense(10), tf.keras.layers.Dense(1), ]) return model def train_func(config: dict): batch_size = config.get("batch_size", 64) epochs = config.get("epochs", 3) strategy = tf.distribute.MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy() with strategy.scope(): model = build_model() model.compile( optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=config.get("lr", 1e-3)), loss=tf.keras.losses.mean_squared_error, metrics=[tf.keras.metrics.mean_squared_error], ) dataset = train.get_dataset_shard("train") for epoch in range(epochs): tf_dataset = dataset.to_tf( feature_columns="x", label_columns="y", batch_size=batch_size ) # verbose=2 shows "X/Y - loss: ..." progress history = model.fit(tf_dataset, callbacks=[ReportCheckpointCallback()], verbose=2) return history.history # Setup config = {"lr": 1e-3, "batch_size": 31, "epochs": 4} train_dataset = ray.data.from_items( [{"x": x / 200, "y": 2 * x / 200} for x in range(2000)] ) scaling_config = ScalingConfig(num_workers=2, use_gpu=False) trainer = TensorflowTrainer( train_loop_per_worker=train_func, train_loop_config=config, scaling_config=scaling_config, datasets={"train": train_dataset}, run_config=RunConfig(storage_path="/tmp/ray_results"), ) result = trainer.fit() ``` Expected Behavior Given: ``` Total samples: 2000 num_workers: 2 batch_size (per-worker config): 31 ``` With Ray Data pre-sharding: ``` Each worker receives: 2000 / 2 = 1000 samples Per-worker batch size: 31 Expected steps per worker: ceil(1000 / 31) = 33 ``` With Pure TensorFlow (no Ray pre-sharding): ``` Each worker loads all 2000 samples Global batch size: 31 * 2 = 62 Steps in one epoch: ceil(2000 / 62) = 33 ``` The code with ray above output: ``` 66/66 [==============================] - 1s 7ms/step - loss: 0.0489 - mean_squared_error: 0.0489 ``` ### Versions / Dependencies Ray version: [2.50.0] TensorFlow version: [2.15.0] ### Issue Severity None

signal.title: [Core] MemoryWatermarkBackpressurePolicy Design
signal.text: ### Description ## 1. Background and Motivation ### 1.1 Problem Statement Ray Data's streaming executor employs a multi-layer backpressure system to prevent Object Store memory exhaustion during pipeline execution. The current system has three policies: | Policy | Mechanism | Limitation | |--------|-----------|------------| | `ConcurrencyCapBackpressurePolicy` | EWMA-based dynamic concurrency cap per operator | Slow to respond to sudden spikes (α=0.1, ~10 rounds to converge) | | `ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy` | Per-operator budget via `ReservationOpResourceAllocator` | Based on Ray Data's internal 50% budget view, blind to external Object Store consumers | | `DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy` | Queue-to-downstream-capacity ratio | Only triggers when budget utilization exceeds 90% — too late | All three policies share a fundamental blind spot: they operate on **Ray Data's internal budget model** (`ResourceManager.get_global_limits()`), which: 1. **Only sees Ray Data's 50% slice** of Object Store (configurable via `DEFAULT_OBJECT_STORE_MEMORY_LIMIT_FRACTION`) 2. **Cannot detect** Object Store pressure from non-Data workloads (Ray Train workers, user Actor objects, etc.) 3. **Has a 1-second cache** that lags behind rapid memory spikes during KubeRay scaling events ```python # Source: resource_manager.py L64-66 DEFAULT_OBJECT_STORE_MEMORY_LIMIT_FRACTION = env_float( "RAY_DATA_OBJECT_STORE_MEMORY_LIMIT_FRACTION", 0.5 ) # Source: resource_manager.py L279-302 def get_global_limits(self) -> ExecutionResources: if time.time() - self._global_limits_last_update_time < self.GLOBAL_LIMITS_UPDATE_INTERVAL_S: return self._global_limits # Returns stale value for up to 1 second ... total_resources = self._get_total_resources() # ↑ Only sees registered nodes; blind to pending nodes during scale-up ``` ### 1.2 Quantified Impact In production KubeRay environments, this blind spot manifests as OOM during scaling: | Scenario | Current Behavior | Consequence | |----------|-----------------|-------------| | KubeRay scale-up (30-120s gap) | `get_global_limits()` returns old cluster size | Object Store fills before new nodes register | | Ray Train + Ray Data co-located | Training actors consume Object Store outside Data's budget | Data's 50% budget overflows actual capacity | | Burst data ingestion | EWMA α=0.1 takes ~10 rounds to track spike | OOM before concurrency cap ramps down | ### 1.3 Design Goals This proposal adds a **MemoryWatermarkBackpressurePolicy** as an emergency circuit breaker: 1. **Absolute watermark**: Monitor `ray.cluster_resources()` directly — independent of `ResourceManager`'s internal budget model 2. **Hysteresis**: Dual watermark (HIGH/LOW) with configurable gap to prevent rapid on/off cycling 3. **Zero deadlock risk**: Only block new task submissions via `can_add_input`; never restrict output reading 4. **Production-grade**: TTL-cached GCS queries, thread-safe state, configurable via `env_float` and `DataContext` ### 1.4 Non-Goals (Scope Out) - **Replacing existing policies**: This is a "last line of defense", not a replacement for the existing three policies - **Adaptive watermarks**: No automatic adjustment of HIGH/LOW based on workload characteristics (future work) - **Per-operator watermarks**: This policy applies a single global watermark; per-operator differentiation is handled by existing policies - **Spilling rate awareness**: No integration with Object Store spill-to-disk metrics --- ## 2. Constraints ### 2.1 Architectural Constraints **C-1: Must implement `BackpressurePolicy` interface** ```python # Source: backpressure_policy.py L14-70 class BackpressurePolicy(ABC): def __init__(self, data_context, topology, resource_manager): ... def can_add_input(self, op) -> bool: return True def max_task_output_bytes_to_read(self, op) -> Optional[int]: return None ``` All backpressure policies must implement this interface. Constructor must use the explicit 3-parameter signature (not `*args, **kwargs`) to match code conventions and enable IDE type checking. **C-2: Must not break the `min` aggregation semantics of `max_task_output_bytes_to_read`** ```python # Source: streaming_executor_state.py L431-451 for policy in backpressure_policies: policy_limit = policy.max_task_output_bytes_to_read(op) if policy_limit is not None: if max_bytes_to_read is None: max_bytes_to_read = policy_limit else: max_bytes_to_read = min(max_bytes_to_read, policy_limit) ``` All policies' `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` values are aggregated via `min()`. A return value of `0` would override the liveness protection in `ReservationOpResourceAllocator` (which returns `1` via `_should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure`), causing `min(1, 0) = 0` — a **deadlock**. **C-3: Must not bypass the `ensure_liveness` fallback mechanism** ```python # Source: streaming_executor_state.py L587-596 if ( not eligible_ops and ensure_liveness and all(op.num_active_tasks() == 0 for op in topology) ): return dispatchable_ops # Fallback: at least 1 op runs to prevent deadlock ``` When all operators are backpressured and no tasks are running, the system forces at least one operator to run. This mechanism only applies to `can_add_input`-based backpressure (operators move to `dispatchable_ops`). The new policy must work within this contract. ### 2.2 Compatibility Constraints **C-4: Must be registrable via `ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES` and `DataContext.set_config`** ```python # Source: backpressure_policy/__init__.py L22-34 ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES = [ ConcurrencyCapBackpressurePolicy, ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy, DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy, ] ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES_CONFIG_KEY = "backpressure_policies.enabled" def get_backpressure_policies(data_context, topology, resource_manager): policies = data_context.get_config( ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES_CONFIG_KEY, ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES ) return [policy(data_context, topology, resource_manager) for policy in policies] ``` Users must be able to enable/disable the policy via `DataContext.set_config`. **C-5: Watermark thresholds must follow existing configurability conventions** All existing policy thresholds use `env_float()` for environment variable overrides: ```python # Example: concurrency_cap_backpressure_policy.py L51 EWMA_ALPHA = env_float("RAY_DATA_CONCURRENCY_CAP_EWMA_ALPHA", 0.1) # Example: downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py L89-91 OBJECT_STORE_BUDGET_UTIL_THRESHOLD = env_float( "RAY_DATA_DOWNSTREAM_CAPACITY_OBJECT_STORE_BUDGET_UTIL_THRESHOLD", 0.9 ) ``` And `DataContext` fields for code-level configuration: ```python # Source: context.py L696-698 downstream_capacity_backpressure_ratio: Optional[float] = DEFAULT_DOWNSTREAM_CAPACITY_BACKPRESSURE_RATIO ``` ### 2.3 Performance Constraints **C-6: GCS RPC overhead must be bounded** `can_add_input(op)` is called for **every operator** in **every scheduling loop iteration** inside a `while True` loop: ```python # Source: streaming_executor.py L476-496 while True: op = select_operator_to_run(topology, self._resource_manager, self._backpressure_policies, ...) if op is None: break topology[op].dispatch_next_task() ``` For a topology with N operators, uncached `ray.cluster_resources()` + `ray.available_resources()` calls would add 2N GCS RPCs per scheduling step. Must cache with TTL matching `ResourceManager.GLOBAL_LIMITS_UPDATE_INTERVAL_S = 1s`. **C-7: Thread safety required** `StreamingExecutor` runs as a daemon thread (`threading.Thread`). The `_throttled` state may be read/written from the scheduling thread while progress reporting reads it from the main thread. --- ## 3. Current State Analysis ### 3.1 Backpressure Execution Path The scheduling loop has two phases per iteration: **Phase 1 — Output reading** (`process_completed_tasks`): Controls how many bytes of completed task outputs can be consumed. All policies' `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` values are aggregated via **min** (most restrictive wins). **Phase 2 — Task submission** (`select_operator_to_run` → `get_eligible_operators`): Controls which operators can submit new tasks. **Any** policy returning `can_add_input=False` blocks the operator (moves it to `dispatchable_ops`). ### 3.2 Liveness Protection Mechanisms Two independent liveness mechanisms exist: | Mechanism | Scope | Trigger | Location | |-----------|-------|---------|----------| | **Task submission liveness** | `can_add_input` | All ops backpressured AND topology fully idle | `streaming_executor_state.py` L587-596 | | **Output reading liveness** | `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` | Budget=0 AND downstream idle/starving | `resource_manager.py` L692-730 (returns `1` via `_should_unblock`) | **Critical insight**: The output reading liveness (returning `1`) can be **overridden** by any policy returning `0` due to `min(1, 0) = 0`. This is the root cause of the deadlock risk in naive implementations. ### 3.3 What Existing Policies Cannot See ``` ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Object Store Memory Layout │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Ray Data Budget │ │ Outside Ray Data's View │ │ │ │ (50% default) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ • Ray Train Actor objects │ │ │ │ ResourceManager │ │ • User ray.put() objects │ │ │ │ can see this │ │ • Other Dataset pipelines │ │ │ │ │ │ • Spill overflow │ │ │ └──────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ MemoryWatermark sees the ENTIRE Object Store via │ │ ray.cluster_resources() / ray.available_resources() │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` --- ## 4. Design ### 4.1 Overall Architecture ```mermaid graph TB subgraph "Scheduling Loop (_scheduling_loop_step)" A["process_completed_tasks()"] B["select_operator_to_run()"] A --> B end subgraph "Phase 1: Output Reading Control" A --> P1["MemoryWatermark.max_task_output_bytes_to_read → None (ALWAYS)"] A --> P2["ResourceBudget.max_task_output_bytes_to_read → N or 1 (liveness)"] A --> P3["ConcurrencyCap/Downstream → None"] P1 --> AGG["min(None, N, None) = N ✓ Liveness preserved"] end subgraph "Phase 2: Task Submission Control" B --> Q1["MemoryWatermark.can_add_input → True/False"] B --> Q2["ConcurrencyCap.can_add_input → True/False"] B --> Q3["ResourceBudget.can_add_input → True/False"] B --> Q4["DownstreamCapacity.can_add_input → True/False"] Q1 --> SHORT["First False → short-circuit, op → dispatchable_ops"] end subgraph "Liveness Fallback" SHORT --> LIVE["All ops backpressured AND all idle → force dispatchable_ops"] end ``` **Key architectural decision**: MemoryWatermark operates **exclusively** through `can_add_input`. It **never** restricts `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` because output reading is the only channel to free Object Store memory. ### 4.2 State Machine ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ NORMAL │ │ can_add_input=True │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ util >= HIGH_WATERMARK (0.85) │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ THROTTLED │ │ can_add_input=False │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ util < LOW_WATERMARK (0.65) │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ NORMAL │ │ can_add_input=True │ │ │ └───────────────────────┘ Hysteresis gap = HIGH - LOW = 20% (prevents rapid cycling) ``` ### 4.3 Core Implementation **File**: `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/memory_watermark_backpressure_policy.py` ```python class MemoryWatermarkBackpressurePolicy(BackpressurePolicy): """Emergency circuit breaker based on absolute Object Store memory utilization.""" # Overridable via env vars and DataContext. DEFAULT_HIGH_WATERMARK: float = env_float("RAY_DATA_MEMORY_WATERMARK_HIGH", 0.85) DEFAULT_LOW_WATERMARK: float = env_float("RAY_DATA_MEMORY_WATERMARK_LOW", 0.65) RESOURCE_QUERY_INTERVAL_S: float = env_float( "RAY_DATA_MEMORY_WATERMARK_QUERY_INTERVAL_S", 1.0 ) def __init__( self, data_context: DataContext, topology: "Topology", resource_manager: "ResourceManager", ): super().__init__(data_context, topology, resource_manager) self._high_watermark = getattr(data_context, "memory_watermark_high", self.DEFAULT_HIGH_WATERMARK) self._low_watermark = getattr(data_context, "memory_watermark_low", self.DEFAULT_LOW_WATERMARK) # Validate: 0 < LOW < HIGH < 1 if not (0.0 < self._low_watermark < self._high_watermark < 1.0): raise ValueError(...) self._throttled: bool = False self._lock = threading.Lock() self._cached_utilization: float = 0.0 self._last_query_time: float = 0.0 ``` **Design decisions embedded in code**: | Decision | Implementation | Rationale | |----------|---------------|-----------| | Explicit 3-param constructor | `__init__(self, data_context, topology, resource_manager)` | Matches `BackpressurePolicy` base class; enables IDE type checking (C-1) | | `getattr` for DataContext fields | `getattr(data_context, "memory_watermark_high", DEFAULT)` | Gracefully falls back when DataContext fields not yet added (C-4) | | `threading.Lock` on `_throttled` | `with self._lock:` in `can_add_input` | Executor runs as daemon thread; prevents race conditions (C-7) | | `time.monotonic()` for cache | `now = time.monotonic()` | Immune to system clock adjustments, unlike `time.time()` | ### 4.4 GCS Query Caching Strategy ```python def _query_utilization(self) -> float: """Query Object Store utilization with TTL caching.""" now = time.monotonic() if now - self._last_query_time < self.RESOURCE_QUERY_INTERVAL_S: return self._cached_utilization # Return cached value within TTL try: cluster = ray.cluster_resources() available = ray.available_resources() total = cluster.get("object_store_memory", 0.0) avail = available.get("object_store_memory", 0.0) if total <= 0.0: return self._cached_utilization # Ray not ready — be permissive util = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - (avail / total))) # Clamp [0, 1] self._cached_utilization = util self._last_query_time = now return util except Exception: # Return CACHED value — NOT 0.0! # 0.0 = "no pressure" = false safety; cached = conservative return self._cached_utilization ``` **Trade-off TD-1: Exception handling returns cached value, not 0.0** Returning `0.0` on GCS failure means "Object Store is empty, allow everything". In a real cluster, GCS unavailability during network partitions or node failures correlates with actual memory pressure. Returning the last known value is the conservative choice — neither false alarm nor false safety. ### 4.5 Output Reading: Why Always `None` ```python def max_task_output_bytes_to_read(self, op) -> Optional[int]: """ALWAYS returns None — never restricts output reading. CRITICAL: The deadlock mechanism if this returned 0: 1. ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy._should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure() detects idle downstream and returns 1 (liveness protection) 2. MemoryWatermark returns 0 3. Aggregation: min(1, 0) = 0 → liveness protection OVERRIDDEN 4. Running tasks complete but output cannot be consumed 5. Object Store memory cannot be freed 6. Utilization stays above HIGH_WATERMARK forever 7. Pipeline DEADLOCKED """ return None ``` This is the single most critical design decision. The deadlock chain: ``` max_task_output_bytes_to_read = 0 (from MemoryWatermark) ↓ min(liveness_unblock=1, watermark=0) = 0 ↓ Output consumption blocked ↓ Object Store memory cannot be freed ↓ Utilization stays above HIGH_WATERMARK ↓ can_add_input stays False ↓ No new tasks + no output consumption = DEADLOCK ``` ### 4.6 Policy Registration Order **File**: `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/__init__.py` ```python ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES = [ MemoryWatermarkBackpressurePolicy, # Position 1: global circuit breaker ConcurrencyCapBackpressurePolicy, ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy, DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy, ] ``` **Trade-off TD-2: MemoryWatermark placed first in the policy list** The scheduling loop short-circuits on the first policy returning `False`: ```python # Source: streaming_executor_state.py L555-558 for p in backpressure_policies: if not p.can_add_input(op): triggered_policy = p.name break # Short-circuit: skip remaining policies ``` When cluster memory is truly critical, MemoryWatermark short-circuits all downstream policies, avoiding unnecessary EWMA calculations and budget lookups. The downside: if MemoryWatermark returns `True` (no pressure), it adds one `_query_utilization()` call (cached, ~0 cost) before other policies run. ### 4.7 DataContext Integration **File**: `python/ray/data/context.py` New constants (alongside `DEFAULT_DOWNSTREAM_CAPACITY_BACKPRESSURE_RATIO`): ```python DEFAULT_MEMORY_WATERMARK_HIGH: float = env_float("RAY_DATA_MEMORY_WATERMARK_HIGH", 0.85) DEFAULT_MEMORY_WATERMARK_LOW: float = env_float("RAY_DATA_MEMORY_WATERMARK_LOW", 0.65) ``` New `DataContext` fields: ```python memory_watermark_high: float = DEFAULT_MEMORY_WATERMARK_HIGH memory_watermark_low: float = DEFAULT_MEMORY_WATERMARK_LOW ``` Three configuration layers (highest priority first): | Layer | Mechanism | Example | |-------|-----------|---------| | 1. Code-level | `DataContext.get_current().memory_watermark_high = 0.75` | Per-pipeline tuning | | 2. Environment variable | `RAY_DATA_MEMORY_WATERMARK_HIGH=0.75` | Cluster-wide default | | 3. Built-in default | `0.85` / `0.65` | Safe out-of-box experience | --- ## 5. Trade-off and Decision Records | ID | Decision Point | Choice | Rationale | Alternative | Risk | |----|---------------|--------|-----------|-------------|------| | TD-1 | Exception handling in `_query_utilization` | Return cached value | Avoids false safety (0.0 = "no pressure") during GCS unavailability | Return 0.0 (permissive) | Stale cache during prolonged GCS outage may block indefinitely; mitigated by `ensure_liveness` fallback | | TD-2 | Policy registration order | First (highest priority) | Short-circuits when memory critical; cached query adds ~0 overhead when not triggered | Last (lowest priority) | Other policies may waste computation before watermark blocks | | TD-3 | `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` | Always `None` | Any non-None value risks overriding liveness protection via `min()` aggregation | Return 0 when throttled | **Deadlock** — output consumption blocked → memory cannot free → permanent throttle | | TD-4 | Watermark scope | Global (entire Object Store) | Detects pressure from non-Data workloads that `ResourceManager` cannot see | Per-operator (like existing policies) | Cannot differentiate operator-specific pressure; mitigated by existing per-operator policies | | TD-5 | Default HIGH=0.85 / LOW=0.65 | 20% hysteresis gap | Balances responsiveness vs stability; 85% leaves 15% headroom for spilling | HIGH=0.80 / LOW=0.60 (more conservative) | May trigger too late if spill rate < production rate; tunable via env vars | | TD-6 | Query cache TTL | 1.0 second | Matches `ResourceManager.GLOBAL_LIMITS_UPDATE_INTERVAL_S` for consistency | Per-scheduling-step (lower latency) | 1s lag acceptable; sub-second queries would overload GCS | | TD-7 | Thread safety mechanism | `threading.Lock` | Simple, correct; contention minimal (lock held only for state check/update) | `threading.RLock` or lock-free atomic | Lock contention negligible in practice; single writer (scheduling thread) | --- ## 6. Known Issues and Risks ### 6.1 Functional Risks | Risk | Probability | Impact | Mitigation | |------|------------|--------|------------| | Watermark triggers too aggressively on shared clusters | Medium | Pipeline throughput reduced unnecessarily | Tunable via `DataContext.memory_watermark_high`; disable via `set_config` | | Stale cache during rapid scale-up causes delayed release | Low | Throttle holds 1s longer than necessary | `RESOURCE_QUERY_INTERVAL_S` is configurable; 1s is acceptable | | `ray.cluster_resources()` returns stale data during GCS leader election | Low | Cached value used (conservative) | `ensure_liveness` prevents deadlock; GCS leader election typically < 5s | | False sense of security: HIGH=0.85 may be too late if spill rate < production | Medium | OOM despite watermark | Phase 0 workaround: lower to 0.75; long-term: integrate spill rate metrics | ### 6.2 Integration Risks | Risk | Probability | Impact | Mitigation | |------|------------|--------|------------| | Breaking change if `BackpressurePolicy.__init__` signature changes | Low | Constructor mismatch | Using explicit params (not `*args/**kwargs`) makes breakage visible at compile time | | Conflict with future `BackpressurePolicy` framework changes (e.g., priority system) | Low | May need refactoring | Minimal internal state; easy to adapt | | Performance regression from additional GCS queries | Very Low | Extra latency per scheduling step | TTL cache limits to 2 RPCs/second regardless of operator count | ### 6.3 Uncovered Scenarios 1. **Multi-pipeline concurrency**: Two Dataset pipelines sharing a cluster will both react to the same global watermark. No coordination between them — both may throttle simultaneously. This is acceptable (conservative) but suboptimal. 2. **Object Store spilling race**: When Object Store is at HIGH_WATERMARK and spilling is active, the watermark may oscillate. The hysteresis gap (20%) is designed to absorb this. 3. **Head-of-line blocking**: MemoryWatermark blocks ALL operators equally. A low-memory operator may be blocked because a different pipeline/workload filled Object Store. Existing per-operator policies handle this partially. --- ## 7. Implementation Plan ### 7.1 General Principles 1. **Zero deadlock**: `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` must NEVER return `0` or any non-`None` value 2. **Backward compatible**: Enabled by default but tunable; existing pipelines see improved safety, not behavioral change under normal conditions 3. **Minimal intrusion**: No changes to `StreamingExecutor`, `ResourceManager`, or existing policies — only adds a new policy class and registration 4. **Observable**: All throttle engage/release events logged at INFO/WARNING level ### 7.2 Phase 1: Core Implementation (1-2 days) **Goal**: Production-ready circuit breaker with full test coverage. **Changed files**: ``` New: python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/memory_watermark_backpressure_policy.py Modified: python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/__init__.py # Register policy python/ray/data/context.py # Add watermark fields New tests: python/ray/data/tests/test_memory_watermark_backpressure_policy.py ``` **Acceptance criteria**: 1. `can_add_input` returns `False` when Object Store utilization >= HIGH_WATERMARK 2. `can_add_input` remains `False` until utilization drops below LOW_WATERMARK (hysteresis) 3. `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` always returns `None` 4. GCS queries cached with TTL=1s; N operators per step triggers at most 1 RPC 5. Exception in `_query_utilization` returns cached value, not 0.0 6. `ValueError` raised if LOW >= HIGH at construction time 7. `DataContext` fields and env vars correctly override defaults 8. Thread-safe under concurrent `can_add_input` calls 9. Registered as first policy in `ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES` 10. `log_once` WARNING on engage, INFO on release ### 7.3 Phase 2: Integration Testing (1 day) **Goal**: Verify no deadlock under simulated memory pressure. **Changed files**: ``` Modified: python/ray/data/tests/test_backpressure_policies.py # Add E2E tests ``` **Test scenarios**: | Test | Setup | Expected | |------|-------|----------| | `test_no_deadlock_under_pressure` | Mock 90% utilization; run `ray.data.range(100).map_batches(...)` | Pipeline completes (liveness fallback works) | | `test_blocks_new_tasks_not_output` | Mock HIGH trigger; verify `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` returns `None` | Output reading unaffected | | `test_hysteresis_prevents_cycling` | Mock util oscillating between 0.70 and 0.80 after trigger | Stays throttled until < LOW | | `test_disable_via_set_config` | Remove from `ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES` via `set_config` | Policy not instantiated | **Acceptance criteria**: 1. All existing `test_backpressure_policies.py` tests still pass 2. New E2E test with mocked high utilization completes without deadlock 3. Pipeline under real load with watermark artificially lowered completes correctly ### 7.4 Phase 3: Production Observability (optional, 1 day) **Goal**: Expose watermark state in Ray Data progress bar and stats. **Changed files**: ``` Modified: python/ray/data/_internal/execution/streaming_executor.py # Add watermark metrics ``` **Acceptance criteria**: 1. `ds.stats()` includes `memory_watermark_throttled_seconds` counter 2. Progress bar shows `[Throttled: MemoryWatermark]` when engaged --- ## 8. Comparison with Existing Policies ### 8.1 Feature Comparison | Dimension | ConcurrencyCap | ResourceBudget | DownstreamCapacity | **MemoryWatermark** | |-----------|---------------|----------------|-------------------|---------------------| | **What it monitors** | Per-op output queue growth (EWMA) | Per-op budget vs allocation | Queue-to-downstream-capacity ratio | **Cluster-wide Object Store utilization** | | **Data source** | Internal metrics | `ResourceManager` budget | `ResourceManager` budget | **`ray.cluster_resources()` (GCS)** | | **Sees non-Data pressure** | No | No | No | **Yes** | | **Response speed** | Slow (α=0.1 EWMA) | Immediate (budget check) | Immediate (threshold check) | **Immediate (threshold check)** | | **Throttle mechanism** | Dynamic concurrency cap | `can_submit_new_task` | `can_add_input` + output limit | **`can_add_input` only** | | **Output reading control** | None | Budget-based with liveness | Returns 0 on backpressure | **None (by design)** | | **Deadlock risk** | None | Protected by `_should_unblock` | Returns 0 → covered by min | **None** | | **Granularity** | Per-operator | Per-operator | Per-operator | **Global** | --- ## Appendix A: Core Source Code Path Index | Module | Path | Key Classes/Functions | |--------|------|----------------------| | Backpressure base class | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/backpressure_policy.py` | `BackpressurePolicy`, `can_add_input`, `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` | | Policy registration | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/__init__.py` | `ENABLED_BACKPRESSURE_POLICIES`, `get_backpressure_policies` | | Concurrency cap policy | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/concurrency_cap_backpressure_policy.py` | `EWMA_ALPHA`, `K_DEV`, `BACKOFF_FACTOR`, `_effective_cap` | | Downstream capacity policy | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py` | `OBJECT_STORE_BUDGET_UTIL_THRESHOLD`, `_should_apply_backpressure` | | Resource budget policy | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/resource_budget_backpressure_policy.py` | `ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy` | | Resource manager | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/resource_manager.py` | `get_global_limits` (L276-299), `DEFAULT_OBJECT_STORE_MEMORY_LIMIT_FRACTION` (L64), `_should_unblock_streaming_output_backpressure` (L692-730), `max_task_output_bytes_to_read` (L896-916) | | Scheduling state | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/streaming_executor_state.py` | `process_completed_tasks` (L431-451), `get_eligible_operators` (L591-636) | | Streaming executor | `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/streaming_executor.py` | `_scheduling_loop_step` (L476-496), `execute` (L166-255) | | Global configuration | `python/ray/data/context.py` | `DataContext`, `downstream_capacity_backpressure_ratio` (L696), `set_config` / `get_config` | | Existing tests | `python/ray/data/tests/test_backpressure_policies.py` | `TestConcurrencyCapBackpressurePolicy`, `_mock_resource_manager` | ### Use case _No response_

signal.title: [<Ray component: Data] [BUG] RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration in StreamingRepartitionRefBundler
signal.text: # [BUG] RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration in StreamingRepartitionRefBundler ## Summary When executing streaming repartition with `write_datasink` on a large Ray cluster, a race condition causes `RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration` error in the progress bar refresh logic. This occurs when concurrent threads attempt to iterate over deques that are being modified simultaneously. ## Environment - **Ray Version**: 2.53.0 - **Python Version**: 3.10 - **Cluster Configuration**: 100 workers × 224 CPUs = 22,400 concurrent tasks ## Issue Description The error occurs during data materialization when using `repartition()` followed by `write_datasink()` operations on large datasets. The failure happens not during the core computation but during progress bar state reporting. ### Minimal Reproducible Example ```python import ray from ray.data import from_pandas import pandas as pd # Initialize Ray cluster with multiple workers ray.init(ignore_reinit_error=True) # Create a large dataset ds = ray.data.range(10000000, parallelism=10000) ds = ds.map_batches(lambda batch: batch * 2, batch_size=1000) # This operation triggers the race condition target_num_rows_per_block = 50000 result = ds.repartition(target_num_rows_per_block=target_num_rows_per_block) # Attempt to materialize - error occurs here try: result.write_datasink(CustomDatasink(...)) # Any datasink operation except RuntimeError as e: print(f"Error: {e}") # RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration ``` ## Root Cause The bug is a **thread-safety race condition** between two concurrent execution paths: ### Path 1: Stream Executor - Adding Bundles (Producer Thread) ``` StreamingExecutor.run() [background thread] └─> Continuously executes stream loop └─> MapOperator processes tasks └─> StreamingRepartitionRefBundler.add_bundle() [Modifies _pending_bundles] └─> Mutates deque: _pending_bundles.append(), _pending_bundles.clear() ``` ### Path 2: Main Thread - Progress Bar Refresh (Consumer Thread) ``` _bundles_to_block_list() [main thread] └─> list(bundles) # Iterating executor └─> StreamingExecutor.get_next() └─> _refresh_progress_bars() [Line 542] └─> OpState.refresh_progress_bar() └─> OpState.summary_str() └─> MapOperator.internal_input_queue_num_bytes() └─> StreamingRepartitionRefBundler.size_bytes() └─> Iterates over _pending_bundles WITHOUT lock [BUG] ``` ### The Race Condition - **Thread 1** (Producer): Calls `add_bundle()` → modifies `_pending_bundles` deque - **Thread 2** (Consumer): Calls `size_bytes()` → iterates over `_pending_bundles` deque WITHOUT acquiring lock - **Result**: `RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration` when the deque is modified during iteration ### Error Stack Trace ``` RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration File "ray/data/_internal/streaming_repartition.py", line 101, in size_bytes return sum(bundle.size_bytes() for bundle in self._pending_bundles) + sum( File "ray/data/_internal/streaming_repartition.py", line 101, in <genexpr> return sum(bundle.size_bytes() for bundle in self._pending_bundles) + sum( ``` The iteration generator is interrupted by `add_bundle()` modifying the deque mid-iteration. ## Fix Applied The fix protects deque iteration with a threading lock to ensure atomicity: ```python def size_bytes(self) -> int: # Create copies of the deques inside the lock to avoid "deque mutated during iteration" # This prevents race conditions when another thread modifies the deques while we're iterating with self._lock: pending_list = list(self._pending_bundles) ready_list = list(self._ready_bundles) # Calculate outside the lock to avoid holding it for too long return sum(bundle.size_bytes() for bundle in pending_list) + sum( bundle.size_bytes() for bundle in ready_list ) ``` **Key Changes**: 1. Acquire `self._lock` before accessing `_pending_bundles` and `_ready_bundles` 2. Create shallow copies of deques as Python lists while holding the lock 3. Release lock before performing expensive `size_bytes()` calculations 4. Iterate over copies, which cannot be mutated by other threads This pattern also applies to `num_blocks()` method for consistency. ## When This Occurs - Large cluster deployments with many concurrent tasks (100+ workers) - High-throughput streaming operations - When progress bar refresh frequency overlaps with bundle addition frequency - Particularly with datasets requiring repartitioning before sink operations ## Status & Verification - **Fixed**: 2026-02-04 - **Affected Version**: 2.53.0 and likely earlier versions - **Verification**: After applying the lock-based fix on 2026-02-04, the error no longer reproduces in subsequent test runs on the same 100-worker cluster configuration. - **Regression Test**: Recommend adding concurrency test case for `StreamingRepartitionRefBundler` with simultaneous add/query operations ## Related Files - `/python/ray/data/_internal/streaming_repartition.py` - Contains `StreamingRepartitionRefBundler` - `/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/streaming_executor.py` - Executor that triggers progress bar refresh - `/python/ray/data/_internal/execution/streaming_executor_state.py` - Progress bar state management ### Issue Severity High: It blocks me from completing my task.

signal.title: [Data] Deprecate ray_remote_args for read APIs
signal.text: ### Description This PR adds named Ray task parameters to read APIs that currently accept `ray_remote_args`: - `label_selector` - `fallback_strategy` - `max_calls` - `resources` - `accelerator_type` - `runtime_env` `ray_remote_args` still works, but now produces a deprecation warning. It will be removed in Ray 2.64. ### Warning behavior Read APIs can call other read APIs, so the warning depth can vary. | Example | Expected behavior | |---|---| | User → `read_datasource` | Warn once and point to the user's call. | | User → `read_csv` → `read_datasource` | Warn once and point to the user's `read_csv` call. | | User → `read_snowflake` → `read_sql` → `read_datasource` | Warn once and point to the user's `read_snowflake` call. | | User → `from_huggingface` → `read_parquet` → `read_datasource` | Don't warn because Ray Data created `ray_remote_args` internally for Parquet retries. The user didn't pass it. | ### Tests | Test | What it checks | |---|---| | `test_read_datasource_ray_remote_args_deprecation_warning` | `read_datasource` produces exactly one warning and points to the caller. | ### Other changes - Updates `from_torch(local_read=True)` to use named parameters. - Updates the read performance documentation. --- Closes https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65500 Closes https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/40673

signal.title: [Data] Refactor: Checkpoint loading from broadcast-join to bucket-join style
signal.text: ## Problem Current checkpoint restore behaves like a **broadcast join**: the full checkpoint (all checkpointed IDs) is loaded once, and the same block ref is passed to every read task via `checkpointed_ids`. Each task filters its input block against this full ID set. **Impact:** - **Slow filtering**: Each task does a full scan / binary search over the entire checkpointed ID set; with large checkpoints this dominates runtime. - **High memory and OOM risk**: Every read task holds a reference to the full checkpoint block; memory scales with parallelism and can cause OOM. - **Resource underutilization**: Downstream operators (e.g. GPU map/write) hold resources but are starved when the read stage is the bottleneck. Goal: switch to a **bucket-join style** so each read task only receives the checkpoint slice for the source path(s) it reads. ## Design principles - **Simplicity**: Keep the checkpoint loading and filtering logic as straightforward as possible. Use the smallest amount of code to load the existing artifacts from checkpoint_path and apply only the necessary, direct filtering. Avoid introducing new branches, new protocols, or multi-step workflows. - **Minimal dependency**: No new config or storage contract; extend existing `checkpoint_path` and infer layout from its contents. - **Backward compatibility**: Flat layout (no subdirs under `checkpoint_path`) keeps current “single full load” behavior. ## Proposed approach: Bucket by source path, load by bucket Partition checkpoint data by a **bucket key** derived from the read source (e.g. file path or directory). - **Write path**: Write checkpoint files under `checkpoint_path/<bucket_key>/` instead of a single flat directory. Rows are grouped by source path (or directory) when writing. - **Load path**: Before execution, each read task’s input paths are known (e.g. from `ReadTask.metadata.input_files`). Load only the checkpoint subdir(s) for those paths and pass each task only the block ref(s) for its bucket(s). **Outcome:** - Each read task gets only the checkpoint slice for its inputs → lower memory per task and faster filtering. - Layout detection: if `checkpoint_path` has subdirectories, use per-bucket loading; otherwise, keep the current single full load (flat layout). ## Compatibility with other datasources (e.g. Kafka) The design only requires a **bucket key** per read task, derived from whatever the datasource puts in `ReadTask.metadata.input_files` (not necessarily a file path): - **Parquet**: `input_files` are file paths; bucket key can be derived from path or parent directory. - **Kafka**: Datasource already sets `input_files` (e.g. `kafka://topic/partition_id`); the same field can be used to derive the bucket key (e.g. by topic or topic+partition). So the load path is compatible with any datasource that sets `input_files`; the write path must bucket checkpoint data using the same key convention. ### Use case _No response_
