signal.title: [Data] Introduce RenameExpr to separate rename semantics from AliasExpr
signal.text: ## Description This PR introduces a dedicated `RenameExpr` type to replace the `_is_rename` flag in `AliasExpr`, providing clearer semantics and better type safety for column renaming operations in Ray Data expressions. **Key Changes:** - Add `RenameExpr` class for explicit column renaming semantics - Remove `_is_rename` flag from `AliasExpr` (now purely for computed columns/aliasing) - Update all 9 visitor implementations to handle `RenameExpr` - Update logical optimization rules for clearer rename vs alias handling - Add comprehensive tests for `RenameExpr` behavior and structural equality **Behavioral Changes:** - `col("a")._rename("b")` now creates `RenameExpr` instead of `AliasExpr` - `col("a").alias("b")` remains `AliasExpr` (semantically correct for aliasing computed expressions) - Projection pushdown now correctly distinguishes rename from alias operations - Rename substitution with non-column expressions downgrades to alias - Rename substitution with aliased columns unwraps the alias and preserves rename semantics **Benefits:** - Resolves the TODO in `_ColumnSubstitutionVisitor` - Makes rename semantics explicit in the type system - Enables future optimizations by separating rename and alias concerns - Improves code clarity and maintainability ## Related issues N/A ## Additional information This refactoring maintains backward compatibility while improving the internal representation. All existing tests pass, and new tests validate the `RenameExpr` behavior including structural equality, evaluation equivalence, and proper handling during column substitution.

signal.title: [Data] Support appending a subset of columns to a Lance dataset.
signal.text: ## Description `Dataset.write_lance(..., mode="append")` fails when the data being appended contains only a subset of the target dataset's columns. On append, the sink sets the write schema to the full existing dataset schema, and the positional `RecordBatchReader.from_batches(schema, ...)` path then errors on the columns the incoming blocks don't provide (`reorder_columns_by_schema` → `Table.select` on a missing field), surfacing as a confusing `LanceError` / `OSError` instead of anything actionable. This PR makes **APPEND** align each block to the dataset schema and **null-fill the columns the block omits** — the missing columns become null for the newly appended rows, analogous to how Iceberg/Delta handle schema evolution on append. If a block contains a column that is *not* in the target dataset, a clear `ValueError` is raised (adding brand-new columns is out of scope; select the existing columns first via `ds.select_columns(...)`). Scope / compatibility: - Only `SaveMode.APPEND` changes. `CREATE` / `OVERWRITE` keep their existing strict behavior (still use `reorder_columns_by_schema`). - No public API change — composes with `ds.select_columns(...)`. - Extension types (e.g. `arrow.json`) and nested types are handled when building the null-filled columns. Before (fails): ```python import ray, lance, pyarrow as pa uri = "/tmp/lance_subset" lance.write_dataset( pa.table({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6], "c": [7, 8, 9]}), uri, mode="overwrite" ) # Data provides only (a, b); the table is (a, b, c) ray.data.from_items([{"a": 10, "b": 40}]).write_lance(uri, mode="append") # -> OSError: LanceError(Arrow): ... KeyError: 'Field "c" does not exist in schema' After (this PR): the append succeeds and the new rows have c = null. Related issues N/A Additional information Tests added in python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_lance.py: test_align_block_to_schema_reorders_fills_and_validates — unit test for the alignment helper: reorders columns, null-fills missing columns, and raises on columns not in the target schema. test_null_column_supports_extension_and_nested_types — null-column construction for extension (arrow.json-like) and nested types. test_lance_write_append_fills_missing_columns_with_null — end-to-end: appending (a, b) rows to an (a, b, c) table writes c as null.

signal.title: [Data] Make logical operator fields canonical
signal.text: ## Description #### Why this is needed: This is the next cleanup in the `#60312` logical plan migration stack. After `Operator` became a thin shared base, `LogicalOperator` can own logical dependencies directly through the public `input_dependencies` contract instead of keeping a separate logical `_input_dependencies` backing field. #### What this PR changes: Makes `LogicalOperator.input_dependencies` the canonical dataclass field for logical inputs and removes the logical `_input_dependencies` backing field. Keeps `name` and `num_outputs` as public logical-operator contracts on `LogicalOperator`: - `name` defaults to the class name, with derived-name operators overriding it through properties or fields. - `num_outputs` defaults to `None`; operators with caller-provided output counts store it as a field, while derived output counts remain properties. Updates the abstract logical map / one-to-one / all-to-all layers to accept `input_dependencies` directly instead of accepting `input_op` and converting it in parent constructors. Stores one-to-one output counts through the public `num_outputs` field instead of `_num_outputs`. `Read` keeps a manual constructor so the existing positional `num_outputs` argument continues to work while still participating in the new field model. Preserves the existing `_get_args()` export key shape, including `_name`, `_num_outputs`, `_input_dependencies`, and `_output_dependencies`, for state/export compatibility. Preserves custom logical-operator fallback rewiring in limit and predicate pushdown by updating copied operators through the frozen-safe `input_dependencies` field. This PR does not change physical operator storage, clean up broader logical-rule special-casing, or change equality/comparability semantics. Those remain separate follow-ups in the current split plan. ## Related issues Part of #60312. ## Additional information This PR corresponds to the logical field-model cleanup step in the current split plan. ### Tests - `pre-commit run --files ...` - Targeted logical plan, state export, limit pushdown, predicate pushdown, read-files logical, and operator fusion tests ### Stack Plan Done: - Convert remaining concrete logical operators to frozen dataclasses. - Make logical abstract classes frozen dataclasses. - Derive logical operator names from the base class. - Replace single-input `input_op` InitVars with `input_dependencies`. - Remove the one-to-one `input_dependency` convenience property. - Clean up logical operator args export. - Make `Operator` a thin shared base. - Consolidate redundant logical operator repr/string logic. This PR: - Make logical operator fields canonical. Next: - Clean up special-casing in logical rules. - Finish equality/comparability end-state.

signal.title: feat: implement arrow string- and binary-view serialization
signal.text: ## Description Allow use of Arrow string-view and binary-view arrays. These were [added in Arrow 1.4](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html#variable-size-binary-view-layout) and, relevant to my interests, are the default string type in [Vortex](https://github.com/vortex-data/vortex), a new columnar file format. ## Related issues Resolves https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/59951 ## Additional information I attempted to adhere to the spirit of this module: elide inaccessible memory. Views, however, make this rather complicated. The out-of-line views are just a buffer index, length, and buffer offset. In theory, multiple views could refer to the same slice of memory or even to overlapping slices. I wrote a naive one-pass algorithm that computes the sum of bytes of the out-of-line views, avoiding double counting when two views refer to the exact same slice. I then check if this estimate of bytes-used is more than half of the buffers' bytes. If it is not, I cast from view to large-(binary/string) and back to view which effectively compacts the buffers. This might not be the best implementation of view serialization but it takes views from not working at all to working.

signal.title: [Data] Improve readability of RefBundle.__repr__
signal.text: The current `RefBundle.__str__` output is hard to read during interactive debugging: - PyArrow schemas show truncated pandas metadata like `'{"index_columns": [], "column_indexes": [], "columns": [{"name":' + 176` - Raw byte counts like `240 bytes` are less readable than human-friendly formats ## What changes were made? - Format PyArrow/Pandas schemas as `{col1: type1, col2: type2}` (omit metadata) - Use `memory_string()` for human-readable byte sizes (B, KiB, MiB, GiB) - Add comprehensive tests for different schema types ## Example **Before:** ``` RefBundle(1 blocks, 12 rows, schema=id: int64 -- schema metadata -- pandas: '{"index_columns": [], "column_indexes": [], "columns": [{"name":' + 176, owns_blocks=False, blocks=( 0: 14 rows, 240 bytes, slice=BlockSlice(start_offset=0, end_offset=12) ) ) ``` **After:** ``` RefBundle(1 blocks, 12 rows, schema={id: int64}, owns_blocks=False, blocks=( 0: 14 rows, 240.0B, slice=BlockSlice(start_offset=0, end_offset=12) ) ) ``` Closes #60694

signal.title: [Data] Add drop parameter to OneHotEncoder and MultiHotEncoder
signal.text: ## Description This PR adds a drop parameter to OneHotEncoder and MultiHotEncoder preprocessors to help prevent multicollinearity when using one-hot encoded features in linear models. Key improvements: - Adds optional drop parameter with three strategies: None (default), "first", and "if_binary" - Implements drop logic for both Pandas and Arrow execution paths - Aligns Ray Data's encoder API with scikit-learn's OneHotEncoder design - Resolves the TODO comment in MultiHotEncoder.__init__ ## Related issues Related to the TODO comment in python/ray/data/preprocessors/encoder.py:657 ## Additional information API Changes Both OneHotEncoder and MultiHotEncoder now accept a drop parameter: ``` def __init__( self, columns: List[str], *, max_categories: Optional[Dict[str, int]] = None, drop: Optional[Literal["first", "if_binary"]] = None, # NEW output_columns: Optional[List[str]] = None, ): ``` ### Parameter behavior: - `drop=None (default)`: Retains all categories (backward compatible) - `drop="first"`: Always drops the first category (alphabetically) - `drop="if_binary"`: Drops first category only when exactly 2 categories exist ### Implementation Details #### OneHotEncoder changes: - Modified _transform_pandas() to apply drop logic after one-hot encoding - Modified _encode_column_one_hot() to handle drop in Arrow execution path - Updated _get_serializable_fields() and _set_serializable_fields() - Updated __repr__() to display drop parameter - Added comprehensive docstring documentation #### MultiHotEncoder changes: - Modified _transform_pandas() to apply drop logic using lambda functions - Updated serialization methods and __repr__() - Removed TODO comment - Added comprehensive docstring documentation

signal.title: [data] fix actor shutdown hooks not being called on UDFs
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? When using `ActorPoolStrategy`, Ray Data actors never call the standard Ray shutdown hook `__ray_shutdown__` on UDF instances. Additionally, `__del__` is only called if a private flag `_enable_actor_pool_on_exit_hook` is manually enabled (which defaults to `False`). This makes it impossible for users to perform cleanup operations when their UDFs are destroyed, which is a common pattern for releasing resources like file handles, database connections, or GPU memory. **Problem** 1. `_enable_actor_pool_on_exit_hook` defaults to `False`, so `on_exit()` is never called 2. Even when enabled, `on_exit()` only deletes the context to trigger `__del__`, but never calls `__ray_shutdown__` **TSolution** 1. **`actor_pool_map_operator.py`**: Modified `on_exit()` to explicitly call `__ray_shutdown__` on all UDF instances before deleting the context 2. **`context.py`**: Changed `_enable_actor_pool_on_exit_hook` default to `True` so cleanup hooks are called by default 3. **`test_map.py`**: Added test to verify both `__ray_shutdown__` and `__del__` are called ## Related issues Fixes #60453

The issue is split into two PRs for easier review. #### This PR focuses on: converting the LogicalOperator hierarchy to frozen dataclasses and making updates immutable via dataclasses.replace. ## Related issues > Link related issues: "Fixes #60312 ", "Closes #60312 ", or "Related to #60312 ". ## Additional information > Optional: Add implementation details, API changes, usage examples, screenshots, etc. #### Implementation details - all logical operators are now `@dataclass(frozen=True)`; - setters/in-place updates become “return-new” methods (e.g., `with_per_block_limit`, `with_detected_parallelism`); - DAG transforms use `dataclasses.replace`; - `__repr__/dag_str` are preserved to keep explain output stable; - inherit_batch_format only applies replace on ops that actually define `_batch_format`; `Read.detected_parallelism` is propagated immutably and the physical planning stage sets the input factory without mutating the logical op. #### API changes logical operators are now immutable; external behavior unchanged; logical layer no longer maintains `_output_dependencies`. #### Tests: logical optimization, planning, and operator-fusion related tests were exercised (see test notes).

signal.title: [Data] Parquet Datasource V2 - regression problem - file extension filtering broken
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen It appears that with 2.57, parquet_datasource_v2 is now the default. This broke our code that uses: ``` ray_data.read_parquet( paths, filesystem=filesystem, schema=schema, file_extensions=None, ) ) ``` ParquetDatasourceV2::__init__ now does: `self._file_extensions = file_extensions or ParquetDatasource._FILE_EXTENSIONS ` and that turns on on filtering with "parquet" when None is provided. The previous and documented behavior of read_parquet is to disable extension filtering if None is passed. See [read_parquet](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/data/api/doc/ray.data.read_parquet.html#read-parquet). The problem shows up when reading files that have no extension. ### Versions / Dependencies 2.57 ### Reproduction script #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Reproduce Ray DataSourceV2 filtering out an extensionless Parquet file. Run with an environment containing Ray Data and PyArrow: python ray_extensionless_parquet_repro.py Expected behavior: Ray reads the Parquet file because ``file_extensions=None`` disables extension filtering. Actual behavior with Ray 2.57.0: ``ray.data.read_parquet`` raises ``ValueError`` with "no files found" because DataSourceV2 applies the default ``parquet`` extension filter. """ from __future__ import annotations import platform import sys import tempfile from pathlib import Path import pyarrow as pa import pyarrow.parquet as pq import ray def main() -> None: print(f"Python: {platform.python_version()}", flush=True) print(f"Ray: {ray.__version__}", flush=True) print(f"PyArrow: {pa.__version__}", flush=True) # Ensure read_parquet uses the DataSourceV2 path where the bug occurs. ray.data.DataContext.get_current().use_datasource_v2 = True ray.init(num_cpus=1, include_dashboard=False) try: with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as temporary_directory: parquet_path = Path(temporary_directory) / "data" table = pa.table({"value": [1, 2, 3]}) pq.write_table(table, parquet_path) assert parquet_path.suffix == "" print(f"Extensionless Parquet file: {parquet_path}", flush=True) print(f"File exists: {parquet_path.is_file()}", flush=True) try: dataset = ray.data.read_parquet( str(parquet_path), file_extensions=None, ) except ValueError as error: print(f"BUG REPRODUCED: {error}", file=sys.stderr, flush=True) raise # Reaching this line means the issue is fixed. print(dataset.take_all()) finally: ray.shutdown() if __name__ == "__main__": main() ### Issue Severity _No response_

signal.title: [Data] Fused map functions are serialized with every shuffle-map task
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen When Ray Data fuses a `MapOperator` into `RandomShuffle` or shuffle-based `Repartition`, the fused upstream map function is stored directly in `ShuffleTaskSpec.map_args`. Pull- and push-based schedulers expand those args into every shuffle-map task submission. A UDF that captures large immutable state is therefore serialized once per shuffle-map task. Currently, a 100 MiB captured closure with 10 input blocks reached about 1004 MiB incremental peak object-store usage in a local pull-shuffle benchmark. The fix reduced the same case to about 104 MiB. The growth is approximately closure size multiplied by map-task count. It should serialize the fused map function once, store it in Ray's object store, and pass its `ObjectRef` as a top-level positional argument to each shuffle-map task. Ray Core should resolve the function before invoking the task. ### Versions / Dependencies on `master` ### Reproduction script ```python import numpy as np import ray state = np.ones(100 * 1024 * 1024, dtype=np.uint8) def udf(batch): assert state[0] == 1 return batch ray.init(num_cpus=4) ( ray.data.range(500_000, override_num_blocks=10) .map_batches(udf, batch_size=None, batch_format="numpy") .random_shuffle(seed=0) .materialize() ) ``` ### Issue Severity Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

signal.title: [Data] Cluster autoscaler requests a bundle larger than the node it was copied from, because node memory is rounded up
signal.text: ## What happened + What you expected to happen ### What happened `DefaultClusterAutoscalerV2.try_trigger_scaling()` builds its resource request by copying whole live nodes out of `ray.nodes()` into `_NodeResourceSpec`, then replicating each node's bundle: ```python node_resource_spec_count = self._get_node_counts() for node_resource_spec, count in node_resource_spec_count.items(): bundle = node_resource_spec.to_bundle() active_bundles.extend([bundle] * count) pending_bundles.extend([bundle] * self._cluster_scaling_up_delta) ``` `_NodeResourceSpec.of()` rounds memory to the nearest 0.1 GiB, and its comment says this is for *grouping*: ```python @classmethod def of(cls, *, cpu=0, gpu=0, mem=0): cpu = math.floor(cpu) gpu = math.floor(gpu) # Round memory to the nearest 0.1 GiB so that nodes of the same type # with slightly different reported physical memory are grouped together. mem = int(round(mem / GiB, 1) * GiB) if mem > 0 else 0 return cls(cpu=cpu, gpu=gpu, mem=mem) ``` But `to_bundle()` re-emits that same rounded value as the resource **request**. Since `round()` goes to nearest, it can round **up**, and the request then describes a node larger than any node in the cluster. The autoscaler correctly reports it cannot be satisfied, and repeats that every few seconds for the entire lifetime of the job: ``` (autoscaler +15s) No available node types can fulfill cluster constraint: {'CPU': 7.0, 'memory': 51432233369.0, 'GPU': 0.0}*3. Add suitable node types to this cluster to resolve this issue. ``` The node those bundles were copied from advertises `memory = 51405389824` — the request is **26,843,545 bytes larger** than the node it describes. Confirmed against the autoscaler's own node-type view (`ray.autoscaler.v2.sdk.get_cluster_status()`), which reports this node type's total as `CPU=7.0, memory=51405389824`: the CPU figure matches the bundle exactly, so memory is the only dimension that overshoots. This is not a niche node size. Over every whole-MiB pod memory limit from 1 GiB to 256 GiB, half of them will produce a request larger than the node, because a value anywhere in the upper half of its 0.1 GiB bucket rounds up. ### What I expected to happen A resource request derived from an existing node's own resources should be satisfiable by that node. Rounding for a **grouping key** should not change the **requested quantity**: flooring to the 0.1 GiB grid preserves the grouping the comment describes (nodes still share a bucket) while never describing a node larger than one that exists. ### Why this matters beyond the log noise The wording is almost identical to a *genuinely actionable* message from the same subsystem: ``` (autoscaler +23s) No available node types can fulfill resource requests {'CPU': 1.0}*5. Add suitable node types to this cluster to resolve this issue. ``` That one reports actors Ray Data cannot place — in our measurements the multiplier is exactly the number of unplaceable actors (`*5` while 5 actors were pending, and absent entirely when the pool was fully placed). Because the infeasible-constraint message above fires continuously and unconditionally, it buries the one that matters. We spent a long time treating both as noise, and missed a real actor-placement problem as a result. ### Additional contributing cause (possibly a separate issue) While verifying the fix on a real cluster I found that flooring the memory alone does **not** silence the warning, because there is a second, independent cause: the request always asks for `count + _cluster_scaling_up_delta` nodes of each shape, and `cap_resource_request_to_limits()` caps that surplus only against `DataContext.execution_options.resource_limits` — never against the worker group's maximum replica count. A group already at its maximum can therefore never satisfy the extra bundle. Measured as a 2x2 on one KubeRay cluster, identical workload in each arm (worker group at `maxReplicas: 2`): | memory floored | `resource_limits` capped | bundle | request > node | warnings in job | |---|---|---|---|---| | no | no | `*3` | yes | 23 | | yes | no | `*3` | no | 23 | | no | yes | `*2` | yes | 22 | | yes | yes | `*2` | no | **0** | Both causes have to be addressed for the symptom to disappear. Happy to split this second one into its own issue if you'd prefer — I've kept it here because a fix to the rounding alone will look ineffective to anyone reproducing the symptom end to end. ## Versions / Dependencies - **Ray**: 2.55.1. I also checked `python/ray/data/_internal/cluster_autoscaler/default_cluster_autoscaler_v2.py` at tags `ray-2.56.0`, `ray-2.56.1`, and on `master`: `_NodeResourceSpec.of()` and `to_bundle()` are byte-identical, so this is still present on master. - **Python**: 3.12.3 - **OS**: Debian-based container image, Linux aarch64 (kernel 6.12) - **Cluster**: KubeRay with `enableInTreeAutoscaling: true` on AKS; head plus two worker pods, worker `resources.limits` of `cpu: 6400m` and `memory: 49024Mi` (the raylet then advertises `CPU: 7.0`, `memory: 51405389824`) - **Ray Data cluster autoscaler**: V2 (the default; `RAY_DATA_CLUSTER_AUTOSCALER` unset) ## Reproduction script The arithmetic reproduces with no cluster and no external dependencies. It calls the same classmethod `try_trigger_scaling()` uses, with the memory value a real KubeRay worker advertises: ```python from ray.data._internal.cluster_autoscaler.default_cluster_autoscaler_v2 import ( _NodeResourceSpec, ) from ray.data._internal.util import GiB # Memory a real KubeRay worker raylet advertises (pod memory limit 49024Mi). advertised = int(47.875 * GiB) # 51405389824 spec = _NodeResourceSpec.of(cpu=7, gpu=0, mem=advertised) requested = spec.to_bundle()["memory"] print(f"node advertises : {advertised}") print(f"bundle requests : {requested}") print(f"difference : {requested - advertised} bytes") assert requested <= advertised, "request is larger than the node it was copied from" ``` Output on Ray 2.55.1: ``` node advertises : 51405389824 bundle requests : 51432233369 difference : 26843545 bytes Traceback (most recent call last): File "repro.py", line 15, in <module> assert requested <= advertised, "request is larger than the node it was copied from" AssertionError: request is larger than the node it was copied from ``` To see the user-visible symptom instead, run any Ray Data job that uses an actor pool on a KubeRay cluster whose worker memory limit is not a whole number of tenths of a GiB (about half of all limits), keep cluster utilisation above the scale-up threshold, and watch the driver log: the `No available node types can fulfill cluster constraint` line repeats every few seconds with a bundle whose `memory` is larger than any node in `ray.nodes()`. ### Suggested fix Floor rather than round when the value will be used as a request, e.g. keep `of()` for the grouping key but have the bundle carry a floored figure: ```python mem = int(math.floor(mem / GiB * 10) * GiB / 10) if mem > 0 else 0 ``` Verified locally: this makes the request equal to or smaller than the source node for every size tested, and still groups nodes whose reported memory differs by less than 0.1 GiB. ### Issue Severity Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.
signal.author: Oblynx

signal.title: [Data] Best practice for data reuse and locality-aware scheduling in rolling-window LightGBM workloads
signal.text: ### Description We would first like to confirm whether Ray already provides a recommended native solution for this workload. If not, this issue describes the capabilities that appear to be missing, particularly reuse across highly overlapping rolling windows, data-local task placement, and memory-aware admission control for independent LightGBM training tasks. ### Use case ## Use case We use Ray to run a large number of independent LightGBM training tasks. A single Ray Job contains approximately 240 Ray Tasks: - Each Task loads a continuous 90-day training window. - Different Tasks use different time windows. - These are usually rolling windows, so adjacent Tasks have significant overlap in their input data. - Each Task independently trains one LightGBM model. - One Job produces approximately 240 models. - These Tasks do not collaboratively train a single distributed LightGBM model. - Each LightGBM model is primarily trained with multithreading on one node. The simplified workload looks like this: ```text Ray Job ├── Task 1: load 90 days of data → train model 1 ├── Task 2: load another 90-day window → train model 2 ├── Task 3: load another 90-day window → train model 3 ├── ... └── Task 240: load another 90-day window → train model 240 ``` For example, if each window moves forward by one day: ```text Task 1: Day 1 to Day 90 Task 2: Day 2 to Day 91 Task 3: Day 3 to Day 92 ... ``` Adjacent Tasks therefore share 89 days of input data. ## Current cluster and execution model Our current environment is approximately: - Ray: 2.56.0 - Python: 3.11.8 - Deployment: KubeRay on Kubernetes - Cluster size: 3 nodes capable of running training tasks - Primary training framework: LightGBM The training dataset is currently small enough to fit into the memory of a single node. To avoid transferring training data between nodes, the application currently uses the following approach: 1. Load a complete copy of the training dataset onto each of the three nodes. 2. Pin different Jobs to specific nodes. 3. Run all training Tasks of a Job primarily on its assigned node. 4. Avoid cross-node data copies by keeping a complete dataset replica on every node. This approach is currently stable: - We have not observed significant Task registration timeout issues. - We have not encountered node OOM failures. - Most cross-node data transfers are avoided. - LightGBM training within a single node is relatively predictable. However, this approach does not fully use Ray as a distributed data and scheduling system. In practice, it is closer to treating the Ray nodes as independent single-node execution environments. ## Problems with the current approach ### 1. The complete dataset may no longer fit into one node As the training dataset grows, it may eventually exceed the memory capacity of a single node. At that point, we will no longer be able to keep a complete copy on every node. We may need to: - Partition the complete dataset into multiple data shards. - Distribute those shards across multiple nodes. - Read multiple shards for one 90-day training window. - Handle windows whose input data spans multiple nodes. This introduces several questions: - What is the appropriate data partitioning granularity? - How can we avoid persistently storing duplicated data for heavily overlapping 90-day windows? - How can a training Task be scheduled on the node that already contains most of its input data? - If a window spans multiple nodes, how should cross-node transfer and temporary memory copies be minimized? - How can we prevent multiple LightGBM Tasks from materializing their inputs simultaneously and causing a node-level OOM? ### 2. Application code currently needs to understand the Ray cluster topology To bind a Job or Task to a node containing a complete copy of the dataset, our application code currently needs to know: - Which nodes exist in the Ray cluster. - Which node contains a particular copy of the dataset. - Which node a Job should be assigned to. - The mapping between application Jobs and Ray nodes. This is manageable with only three nodes. As the cluster grows, however, this creates several problems: - Application code becomes coupled to the deployment topology. - Scaling events and node failures may require changes to node-binding logic. - Application developers need to understand Ray node identifiers, resources, and scheduling configuration. - Different Jobs may repeatedly implement similar data-location and Task-scheduling logic. - Manually maintaining the mapping between Jobs and nodes will become difficult. Ideally, application code should only need to describe: ```text This Task requires this date range, these columns, and these training parameters. ``` It should not need to describe: ```text This Task must run on this specific Ray node. ``` ## Desired behavior Ideally, application code would declare a training window such as: ```python window = { "start_date": "2026-01-01", "end_date": "2026-03-31", "columns": [...], } ``` Ray or a data management layer would then automatically: 1. Identify the data shards required by the window. 2. Determine which nodes currently hold those shards. 3. Select a node that has most of the required data and sufficient resources. 4. Schedule the training Task on that node. 5. Transfer only the missing shards. 6. Reuse data shared by overlapping windows. 7. Limit the number of concurrent LightGBM Tasks per node to prevent OOM. 8. Recalculate data placement and Task placement after node scaling or failure. 9. Hide the concrete Ray cluster topology from application code. ## Questions for the community ### 1. Does Ray already provide a native solution for this workload? We are aware of several potentially relevant Ray capabilities: - Ray Core locality-aware scheduling - Object storage and cross-node transfer through the Ray Object Store - Ray Data block management, streaming execution, backpressure, and locality scheduling - Ray Train `LightGBMTrainer` - Ray Tune concurrency and resource management - Placement Groups, Node Affinity, Node Labels, and custom resources However, we are unsure how these capabilities should be combined for this workload. In particular: - Can Ray Data automatically manage highly overlapping rolling time windows and reuse data shared by adjacent windows? - When a training Task depends on multiple `ObjectRef`s or Ray Data blocks, does Ray automatically schedule the Task on the node containing the largest number of local input bytes? - If the data for one 90-day window is distributed across multiple nodes, what is the recommended Ray execution model? - For 240 independent LightGBM models, should we use ordinary Ray Tasks, Ray Tune, or Ray Train `LightGBMTrainer`? - Is `LightGBMTrainer` mainly intended for multiple workers collaboratively training one model, rather than one Job training 240 independent models? - Does Ray provide a native mechanism to limit per-node training concurrency based on worker heap memory or the actual memory usage of LightGBM? ### 2. Should users manage data partitioning themselves? If we use Ray Data, would the recommended approach be to: - Convert the complete dataset into a Ray Dataset. - Allow Ray Data to generate and manage its blocks. - Filter the Dataset by date for each training window. - Convert each window into pandas, NumPy, or `lightgbm.Dataset` inside the training Task. For a large number of highly overlapping windows, would this repeatedly perform filtering, materialization, and Arrow-to-LightGBM conversion? Is there a recommended caching or reuse mechanism that avoids independently loading the same underlying data for all 240 windows? ### 3. Should users implement a data-location directory and scheduling layer? We are exploring a lightweight coordination layer with the following flow: ```text Canonical time-based data shards ↓ Track the nodes holding each shard ↓ Combine multiple shards into a logical 90-day window ↓ Select the node containing most of the window data ↓ Apply per-node LightGBM memory admission control ↓ Submit an ordinary Ray Task to train one model ``` This coordination layer might be responsible for: - Maintaining a data-shard directory. - Managing cached data and its lifecycle. - Mapping rolling windows to their underlying shards. - Selecting the Task execution node based on local data volume. - Applying per-node LightGBM training memory admission. - Submitting Tasks in bounded waves instead of starting all 240 Tasks at once. We would like to understand: - Would this duplicate functionality already provided by Ray Data or Ray Core? - Should this be implemented as an extension around Ray Data rather than by independently managing Arrow `ObjectRef`s? - Is there an existing Ray API for querying the node distribution of `ObjectRef`s or Ray Dataset blocks? - Is there a recommended way to express both data-location preference and node-memory safety to the Ray scheduler? - If an application-level coordination layer is necessary, what should the responsibility boundary be between that layer, Ray Core, and Ray Data? ### 4. How should actual LightGBM memory consumption be handled? Our training input may initially be stored as Arrow data, but LightGBM training usually involves additional materialization: ```text Arrow → pandas / NumPy → lightgbm.Dataset → LightGBM internal binning and training structures ``` As a result, the peak memory usage of a Task may be significantly larger than the original Arrow input size. Ray CPU resource declarations can limit the number of concurrent Tasks, but we are unsure about the recommended way to limit LightGBM Task concurrency based on node memory: ```text Safe concurrency per node = min( concurrency allowed by available CPUs, concurrency allowed by available memory ) ``` We would like guidance on the following: - Does Ray recommend using a custom logical resource to represent training memory? - Should Ray memory monitoring and OOM prevention be used as the primary concurrency-control mechanism? - Should bounded concurrency be implemented at the application level using `ray.wait()`? - Can Ray Data backpressure account for worker heap memory consumed after data is materialized into a `lightgbm.Dataset`? - Is there a recommended admission-control pattern for workloads with significant and workload-dependent memory amplification? ## Approach we are currently considering Our current direction is: 1. Partition unique time-series data into reusable Arrow shards. 2. Avoid permanently storing one complete physical copy for every 90-day window. 3. Represent each training window as a logical reference to multiple underlying shards. 4. Prefer nodes containing the largest portion of the required window data. 5. Let Ray Core handle actual Task execution and object transfer. 6. Train one model per Task using single-node multithreaded LightGBM. 7. Limit concurrent training Tasks according to each node’s available memory. 8. Execute the 240 Tasks in bounded waves. 9. Keep node IDs and cluster topology hidden from application code. At the same time, we are locally exploring a lightweight data scheduling framework. Before investing further, we would like to confirm whether Ray already provides a more native, simpler, or recommended solution. ## Guidance we are looking for We would appreciate the community’s guidance on the following: 1. What is the recommended Ray stack for this workload? 2. Can Ray Data directly address rolling-window data reuse and data-local scheduling? 3. Should 240 independent LightGBM models be executed using ordinary Ray Tasks, Ray Tune, or Ray Train? 4. Do users need to maintain the locations of data shards themselves? 5. Do users need to implement their own compute-follows-data scheduling? 6. How can data-local scheduling be exposed without making application code aware of cluster topology? 7. How should per-node LightGBM Task concurrency be limited to avoid worker heap OOM? 8. If an extension is required, should it be built around Ray Data, Ray Core scheduling, or an independent data coordination layer? Our goal is to reuse Ray’s native capabilities wherever possible and avoid rebuilding functionality that Ray already provides.
signal.author: quenlang007-create

signal.title: [Data] write_lance is incompatible with PyLance 6.x due to removed storage_options_provider argument
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen ## Description Ray 2.55.1 passes the keyword argument `storage_options_provider` to PyLance write APIs, but PyLance removed that argument https://github.com/lance-format/lance/pull/6186 and replaced it with `namespace_client` / `table_id`. As a result `Dataset.write_lance()` fails with newer versions of lance: ```text TypeError: write_fragments() got an unexpected keyword argument 'storage_options_provider' ``` ## Reproduction ```python import ray ds = ray.data.from_items([{"id": 1, "text": "a"}, {"id": 2, "text": "b"}]) ds.write_lance("/tmp/ray-lance-test") ``` Actual: ```text ray.exceptions.RayTaskError(TypeError): ray::Write() TypeError: write_fragments() got an unexpected keyword argument 'storage_options_provider' ``` Expected: the dataset is written, or Ray fails fast with a clear version-compatibility error. ## Root cause In `/ray/data/_internal/datasource/lance_datasink.py` the argument is passed unconditionally, even when no namespace is configured and the provider is `None` (lines 130-150): ```python storage_options_provider = create_storage_options_provider( namespace_impl, namespace_properties, table_id ) write_fragments( reader, uri, ..., storage_options=storage_options, storage_options_provider=storage_options_provider, ) ``` Three call sites are affected, so fixing only `write_fragments()` would leave the append and commit paths broken: | Line | Call | | --- | --- | | 149 | `write_fragments(..., storage_options_provider=...)` | | 250 | `lance.LanceDataset(..., storage_options_provider=...)` (APPEND) | | 306 | `lance.LanceDataset.commit(..., storage_options_provider=...)` | All three PyLance targets dropped the parameter in 6.x: | PyLance 6.0.1 API | `storage_options_provider` | `namespace_client` | | --- | --- | --- | | `write_fragments` | absent | present | | `LanceDataset.__init__` | absent | present | | `LanceDataset.commit` | absent | present | ## Affected versions Inspected the Python / `.pyi` sources of each published wheel: | PyLance | `storage_options_provider` | | --- | --- | | 6.0.0 – 9.0.0 (latest) | **absent** | ## Suggested fix Support the current PyLance API by selecting `storage_options_provider` vs `namespace_client` / `table_id` based on the installed signature at all three call sites, and omit the namespace argument entirely for plain URI writes. ### Versions / Dependencies ray==2.55.1 pylance==6.0.1 ### Reproduction script ```python import ray ds = ray.data.from_items([{"id": 1, "text": "a"}, {"id": 2, "text": "b"}]) ds.write_lance("/tmp/ray-lance-test") ``` ### Issue Severity Low: It annoys or frustrates me.
signal.author: allvphx

signal.title: [Data] ray.data.read_delta silently drops columns on Delta tables with column mapping enabled
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen `ray.data.read_delta` silently produces an incorrect schema when reading a Delta table that has **Delta Column Mapping** enabled. Columns added after column mapping was enabled are stored in the physical parquet files using UUID-based physical names (e.g. `col-4d014c4b-7d15-4d7b-a89e-blah-blah`). The Delta log contains the mapping from these UUIDs to logical column names, but `ray.data.read_delta` does not apply this translation. As a result, the returned dataset's schema contains UUID column names for those columns rather than their logical names, and any attempt to select or cast those columns by their logical name raises a `KeyError`. ## Root Cause Chain 1. `ray.data.read_delta` calls `DeltaTable(path, version=version).file_uris()` from `deltalake` to get parquet paths, then passes them to `ray.data.read_parquet`. 2. `ray.data.read_parquet` infers the dataset schema from `pq_ds.fragments[0].physical_schema` — the first parquet file's raw schema. 3. For a column-mapping-enabled Delta table, the physical parquet file stores columns using UUID names. The logical name translation lives in the Delta log metadata, which `deltalake 1.6.1` does not apply to the physical schema exposed to Ray. 4. The resulting dataset schema contains `col-4d014c4b-7d15-4d7b-a89e-<redacted> double` where `<string column_name> double` is expected. ## Observed Schema (excerpt) ``` is_2_way bool ← last logical name col-4d014c4b-7d15-4d7b-a89e-40dfdca76a22 double ← should be a logical name col-8c0bb653-f5db-4b02-a361-d29086e7f2ed double ... _row-id-col-9e9b0ae3-... int64 _row-commit-version-col-7bc4f86e-... int64 ``` - `DESCRIBE TABLE` confirms real column name exists at ordinal position 356 with type `double` - `SHOW TBLPROPERTIES` confirms `delta.columnMapping.mode` is enabled on the table - `DESCRIBE HISTORY` shows no `ADD COLUMN` operations — the column has existed since table creation; only its physical representation changed when column mapping was enabled - Downgrading `deltalake` to `0.x` (which applied column mapping translation correctly) resolves the issue ## Expected Behavior `ray.data.read_delta` should apply the Delta log's column mapping metadata to translate physical UUID column names to their logical names before constructing the dataset schema, consistent with how `deltalake 0.x` and Databricks' native readers behave. ## Further diagnostics Per Anyscale's suggestion, we supplied a schema on read: ```python dt = DeltaTable("s3://my-bucket/my-table", storage_options={"AWS_REGION": "...}) col_map = { field.metadata.get("delta.columnMapping.physicalName", field.name): field.name for field in dt.schema().fields } ds = ray.data.read_unity_catalog(...) ds = ds.rename_columns(col_map) ``` This fixes reads (though ideally would not be required), but is incompatible with adding `row_filter`s to read_unity_catalog calls because row filters using logical table names are not mapped to the physical column name. The filter is then silently ignored, causing a full table scan. Per Anyscale, it seems like we should've hit [this](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-rs/blob/main/python/deltalake/table.py#L1023) error from deltalake, but did not. ### Versions / Dependencies - Ray: 2.55.1 - deltalake: 1.6.1 - PyArrow: 21.0.0 - Python: 3.11 ### Reproduction script Nontrivial to reproduce in isolation as this requires a databricks table with column mapping. ### Issue Severity None

signal.title: [Ray Data] Is there any plan to support Hive on Ray or a Hive-compatible SQL execution backend?
signal.text: ### Description ### Problem / Motivation Many large-scale data warehouse environments still rely heavily on Hive tables, Hive Metastore, and Hive SQL workloads. Today, common execution engines for Hive SQL include MapReduce, Tez, and Spark. Meanwhile, Ray Data is becoming increasingly attractive for large-scale data processing, especially for Python-native, AI/ML, batch inference, feature engineering, and GPU-heavy pipelines. I would like to ask whether the Ray community has any plan, interest, or design direction around supporting a "Hive on Ray" model, or more generally, a Hive-compatible SQL execution layer on top of Ray / Ray Data. By "Hive on Ray", I mean one of the following possible directions: 1. A true Hive execution engine backend where Hive physical plans can be executed by Ray. 2. A SQL-on-Ray layer that can query Hive Metastore tables and execute SQL using Ray Data / Ray Core. 3. A Ray Data integration that makes it easy to read/write Hive tables, preserve Hive partition semantics, and gradually support SQL-like workloads. The core question is: > Is there any roadmap or recommended architecture for running Hive-style SQL workloads on Ray? --- ### Why this matters Spark is currently a common choice for executing Hive SQL or Spark SQL workloads. However, some workloads are becoming increasingly Python-heavy and AI-native, for example: - Large-scale batch inference - Embedding generation - Feature engineering - Multi-modal data processing - Python UDF-heavy ETL - CPU + GPU mixed data pipelines - Data preprocessing before model training For these workloads, Ray has several natural advantages: - Python-first programming model - Better integration with Ray Train, Ray Serve, Ray Tune, and distributed actors - More flexible CPU/GPU/custom resource scheduling - Better fit for model inference and AI data pipelines - Easier model loading and reuse through actors However, many enterprise data platforms still use Hive Metastore and Hive tables as the source of truth. Without strong Hive compatibility, adopting Ray Data in existing data warehouse pipelines can require extra glue code and migration effort. ### Use case #### Use Case 1: Run SQL over Hive tables using Ray Users have existing Hive tables such as: ```sql SELECT city_id, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS user_cnt, SUM(pay_amount) AS pay_amount FROM dwd_order_detail WHERE dt = '2026-07-10' GROUP BY city_id; ``` Today this may run on Hive on Tez or Spark SQL. The desired future state is to execute this type of SQL using Ray as the distributed execution backend, while still reading metadata from Hive Metastore and data from HDFS/S3/object storage. Potential user experience could be something like: -- hypothetical SET hive.execution.engine=ray; or a separate SQL-on-Ray service that supports Hive Metastore catalogs. --- Use Case 2: Migrate PySpark ETL to Ray Data while preserving Hive table semantics Many existing ETL jobs are written in PySpark mainly because Spark integrates well with Hive tables and Hive Metastore. A Ray-native replacement would ideally support: - Reading Hive table partitions - Partition pruning, for example dt = '2026-07-10' - Reading common formats such as Parquet and ORC - Writing back to Hive-compatible partitioned directories - Registering or refreshing Hive partitions - Preserving schema and table metadata as much as possible This would make it easier to migrate from PySpark to Ray Data for Python-heavy data processing.
signal.author: JiGuoDing

signal.title: [Data] Support incremental reads for Iceberg tables
signal.text: ### Description ### What would you like to see added? Ray Data currently supports reading an Iceberg table via `ray.data.read_iceberg(...)`, including reading a specific snapshot with `snapshot_id`. However, it does not appear to expose Iceberg's incremental read capability for reading data between two snapshots. It would be useful for Ray Data to support incremental reads for Iceberg tables, for example by allowing users to read appended rows between a start snapshot and an end snapshot. PyIceberg has implemented incremental append scan support in apache/iceberg-python#3512: https://github.com/apache/iceberg-python/pull/3512 That PR adds `Table.incremental_append_scan(...)`, which can scan rows appended by append snapshots within a snapshot range. ### Why is this needed? Many data pipelines only need to process newly appended Iceberg data since the last processed snapshot. Without native support in Ray Data, users need to manually inspect Iceberg snapshot history/manifests or read full snapshots and compute diffs externally, which is inefficient and error-prone. Native support would make it easier to build incremental ETL and ML data processing pipelines on top of Ray Data and Iceberg. ### Possible API One possible direction is to extend `ray.data.read_iceberg(...)` with incremental scan options, such as: ```python ray.data.read_iceberg( table_identifier="db.table", catalog_kwargs={...}, start_snapshot_id=..., # exclusive or inclusive depending on Iceberg semantics end_snapshot_id=..., ) Alternatively, Ray Data could expose a separate API such as ray.data.read_iceberg_incremental(...). Additional context Current Ray Data Iceberg support passes snapshot_id to PyIceberg Table.scan(), which enables reading a specific snapshot but not reading the delta between snapshots. Since PyIceberg now has incremental append scan support, Ray Data could potentially build on top of that functionality. cc @ray-project/data ``` ### Use case _No response_
signal.author: neuyilan

signal.title: [Data] Feature request: row-level filename control in write APIs (migration path from `get_filename_for_row()`)
signal.text: ### Description `get_filename_for_row()` on `FilenameProvider` has been deprecated in #61821 in favour of `get_filename_for_task()`, with no supported alternative for producing **per-row output filenames**. We understand the motivation: 2PC recovery requires deterministic, task-level filename prefixes so that checkpoint IDs can map 1:1 to data file prefixes. However, the deprecation removes a capability with **no clear migration path** for users who need row-level output filenames. `get_filename_for_task()` produces a single filename per task (or per block). It has no access to individual row data. Row-level output filenames are needed whenever each row maps to a uniquely-identifiable output file (per-document, per-image, per-UUID), output must conform to an existing directory structure convention, or the dataset is written to a data lake where downstream consumers expect a specific path layout per record. These are common patterns in ML data pipelines, particularly for image/media processing at scale. We would like one of: 1. **Keep `get_filename_for_row()` as a supported API**, perhaps with an opt-out from 2PC recovery (since row-level writes are inherently not 1:1 with task checkpoints anyway). 2. **Provide a new row-level write API** — e.g., a callback or `map`-style writer that gives per-row filename control while still benefiting from Ray Data's write infrastructure. 3. **Document the recommended migration path** if neither of the above is planned. The deprecation warning doesn't explain what to do instead when row-level filenames are needed. ### Use case We run batch image processing pipelines with `ray.data`. Each row in our dataset corresponds to a single media asset identified by a UUID. When writing outputs, each row must produce a file at a path derived from that row's UUID: ```python class MediaFilenameProvider(FilenameProvider): def get_filename_for_row(self, row, write_uuid, task_index, block_index, row_index): return f"media/{row['media_uuid']}/image.png" ``` Used with: ```python dataset.write_images( output_path, column="image", filename_provider=MediaFilenameProvider(), filesystem=fs, ) ``` This directory structure (`media/<uuid>/image.png`) is a convention enforced by our downstream systems, we cannot change it. The output filename **must** be derived from row data, not from the task index. Our requirement is N rows in a batch -> N output files, each named after its row's UUID. The only workaround we see is replacing `write_images()` with a `map_batches()` that manually writes each file using the filesystem directly. This works but loses all of Ray Data's write optimizations (backpressure, retries, checkpointing), requires reimplementing file I/O and error handling, and defeats the purpose of having a `write_images()` API.

signal.title: [Data] Support predicate pushdown at Delta Lake level
signal.text: ### Description Instead of immediately resolving the parquet file URIs from a DeltaLake table, defer their resolution until execution to enable filtering based on the delta table metadata. This would likely involve a new DeltaDatasource. ### Use case Currently when using `read_delta`, the table is immediately resolved to a list of parquet URIs that are passed into `read_parquet`. If the dataset does not use Hive partitioning, but rather Delta's built-in Z-ordering and table metadata, you end up potentially reading a bunch of unnecessary files, even if it's just for the tail metadata. What would be preferable is deferring this resolution until the source is actually read, at which point all predicates that have been pushed down to the source can be passed to the `file_uris` call. Other attributes such as the schema could also be [efficiently retrieved](https://delta-io.github.io/delta-rs/usage/examining-table/#schema) using Delta Lake-native methods as opposed to the "bunch of parquet files" mode.

signal.title: [data] ObjectRefs passed to map UDF are not automatically deref'ed
signal.text: When users pass an ObjectRef as a UDF parameter. It's supposed to be automatically deref'ed ```python def map_fn(arg): # The following is broken right now. # assert arg == 1 # Instead, users need to use arg = ray.get(arg) arg_ref = ray.put(1) ds.map(map_fn, fn_args=[arg_ref]) ``` This bug hurts both user experience and performance. Because the UDF arguments are not passed as the Ray task arguments. So Ray Scheduler doesn't know if the arguments are ready or not, before scheduling the tasks.

signal.title: [Ray Data] Categorizer throws internal errors during doctest
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen The preprocessor class `ray.data.preprocessors.Categorizer` shows unexpected behavior: When running the doctests, the second one (where you specify the dtype as pd.Categorical), an internal TypeError is thrown: ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "/Users/A1A6EB8/Library/Caches/pypoetry/virtualenvs/capacity-utilization-ml-JEcJSmHA-py3.11/lib/python3.11/site-packages/ray/data/dataset.py", line 5631, in types arrow_types.append(pa.from_numpy_dtype(dtype)) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "pyarrow/types.pxi", line 5708, in pyarrow.lib.from_numpy_dtype TypeError: Cannot interpret 'CategoricalDtype(categories=['female', 'male'], ordered=False, categories_dtype=object)' as a data type 2025-02-06 12:18:02,280 ERROR dataset.py:5635 -- Error converting dtype category to Arrow. Traceback (most recent call last): File "/Users/A1A6EB8/Library/Caches/pypoetry/virtualenvs/capacity-utilization-ml-JEcJSmHA-py3.11/lib/python3.11/site-packages/ray/data/dataset.py", line 5631, in types arrow_types.append(pa.from_numpy_dtype(dtype)) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "pyarrow/types.pxi", line 5708, in pyarrow.lib.from_numpy_dtype TypeError: Cannot interpret 'CategoricalDtype(categories=['L3', 'L4', 'L5', 'L6'], ordered=True, categories_dtype=object)' as a data type ``` This internal error is eventually catched, since the tests terminates with exit code 0. However, the expected output of the test, which is given as ``` >>> categorizer.fit_transform(ds).schema().types # doctest: +SKIP [CategoricalDtype(categories=['female', 'male'], ordered=False), CategoricalDtype(categories=['L3', 'L4', 'L5', 'L6'], ordered=True)] ``` does not equal the actual output, which is `[None, None]`. ### Versions / Dependencies Python: 3.11.6 Ray: 2.42.0 OS: MacOS ### Reproduction script See also doctest of class: ```import pandas as pd import ray from ray.data.preprocessors import Categorizer if __name__ == "__main__": df = pd.DataFrame({"sex": ["male", "female", "male", "female"], "level": ["L4", "L5", "L3", "L4"]}) ds = ray.data.from_pandas(df) categorizer = Categorizer( columns=["sex", "level"], dtypes={"level": pd.CategoricalDtype(["L3", "L4", "L5", "L6"], ordered=True)} ) categorizer.fit_transform(ds).schema().types ``` ### Issue Severity Low: It annoys or frustrates me.

signal.title: [docs][core] Document JVM signal conflicts with PyArrow HDFS
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? On Linux, PyArrow HDFS loads `libhdfs`, which embeds a HotSpot JVM in the Python process. HotSpot uses some `SIGSEGV` events as recoverable VM control flow, while Ray's CoreWorker installs an Abseil failure-signal handler that can interpret the same signal as a fatal native crash. The conflict can be established during handler installation and surface later as an intermittent JVM crash. This PR documents: - the symptoms and root cause of the Ray/PyArrow HDFS signal-handler conflict; - HotSpot signal chaining with `libjsig.so` as the preferred mitigation because it keeps Ray's native crash diagnostics enabled; - `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER=1` as a fallback and its diagnostic trade-off; - the process-start timing requirement for `LD_PRELOAD` and a KubeRay configuration example; - discoverable entry points from the Ray Data and Ray Train HDFS documentation. Related to #36415. ## Duplicate-work check I reviewed #36415 and searched open PRs for the issue number, `libjsig`, and PyArrow/HDFS signal-handler documentation. I found no open PR covering this documentation work. #58984 is already merged and added `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER`, but it didn't document the option, its diagnostic trade-off, or HotSpot signal chaining. ## Validation Documentation checks: - `git diff --check` - `python -m pre_commit run --files doc/source/ray-observability/user-guides/debug-apps/debug-failures.rst doc/source/train/user-guides/persistent-storage.rst doc/source/data/loading-data.rst` - `sphinx-lint --disable trailing-whitespace doc/source/ray-observability/user-guides/debug-apps/debug-failures.rst doc/source/train/user-guides/persistent-storage.rst doc/source/data/loading-data.rst` - `./ci/lint/lint.sh documentation_style` (`0 errors, 0 warnings`) - Verified the linked Oracle signal-handling pages and #36415 return HTTP 200. - Validated the documented `find`/`LD_PRELOAD` shell snippet with the local OpenJDK 17.0.19 installation. Runtime validation behind the guidance: - Reproduced the unmitigated JVM termination and generated multiple `hs_err_pid*.log` files. - Completed 5,000- and 10,000-operation HDFS stress runs with `RAY_DISABLE_FAILURE_SIGNAL_HANDLER=1` without reproducing the crash. - Completed a 5,000-operation HDFS stress run with only `libjsig.so` preloaded and Ray's handler left enabled. - Completed a separate 1,000-operation `libjsig.so` run, followed by a clean `ray.shutdown()` and process exit code 0. The full Sphinx documentation site wasn't built locally because the existing Python environment doesn't include the Ray documentation dependency set. The Read the Docs preview build provides full-site validation. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate the failure, draft the documentation, and run the validation commands. I reviewed every changed line and the reported test results.

signal.title: [Data] Deprecate min_rows_per_file with partitioned parquet writes
signal.text: ## Description `min_rows_per_file` can't guarantee a minimum file size with `partition_cols`: each block can be split across partition directories, and no single write task necessarily sees all rows of a partition. Per the maintainer decision in [#59485](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/59485), deprecate the combination instead of silently ignoring the hint. This follows up on [#53930](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/53930), where the combination works when each partition fits in one write task. To avoid a hard behavior break, passing both options now emits a `DeprecationWarning` and retains the existing behavior. Users who repartitioned by the partition columns can remove `min_rows_per_file` without changing the output layout. ## What changed? - Emit a `DeprecationWarning` when `write_parquet` is called with both non-empty `partition_cols` and `min_rows_per_file`. - Apply the same warning to the deprecated `num_rows_per_file` alias. - Keep `partition_cols=[]` allowed, since it doesn't enable partitioned writes. - Update the `write_parquet` docstring and Ray Data docs with the migration guidance. - Update the tests to verify the warnings, successful writes, the deprecated alias, and the empty-list edge case. ## Related issues Related to [#59485](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/59485)

signal.title: [Core][GCS] Export Redis payload byte metrics by command and table
signal.text: ### Description ### What happened + What you expected to happen GCS Redis command latency and count do not explain whether load is caused by many small values or a few very large payloads. Operators need request and response payload byte metrics to identify table growth, expensive scans, and oversized records. We expect counters for bytes sent to and received from Redis, labeled by a bounded command category and GCS table name. The metric definition must state whether key bytes, protocol overhead, compressed bytes, and returned field names are included. Recording must occur before request buffers are moved and after response parsing while sizes are still available. ### Use case An operator observing Redis memory growth or GCS latency can calculate average read payload size per table: ``` sum by (TableName) ( rate(ray_gcs_redis_response_payload_bytes_total{ Command=~"HGET|HMGET|HSCAN" }[5m]) ) / sum by (TableName) ( rate(ray_gcs_redis_command_count{ Command=~"HGET|HMGET|HSCAN" }[5m]) ) ``` This separates high operation volume from unusually large records without requiring invasive Redis commands such as `MONITOR`, `MEMORY USAGE`, or `--bigkeys`, which may be unavailable on managed Redis services.

signal.title: [ci] Resolve packages through the mirror in the manylinux image too
signal.text: **Stacked on #65571** — base branch is `elliot-barn/pypi-mirror-integration`, since the proxy and the profile.d script land there. Review after that one; GitHub will retarget this to master when it merges. ## Description Steps whose `job_env` is `manylinux-x86_64` had none of the mirror wiring, because it lived only in `forge.Dockerfile`. Audited on premerge 72104: | Step runs in | Mirror used? | Examples | |---|---|---| | forge | yes — probe logs the verdict, zero direct PyPI fetches | reef tooling, lints, test-rules, `ml: train minimal`, `serve: wheel tests` | | manylinux-x86_64 | **no wiring at all** | **`build: raydepsets: compile all dependencies`**, `build: jar`, wheel builds | That gap is what failed the build: uv fetched `numpy-2.2.6-…whl.metadata` straight from `files.pythonhosted.org` and took a 502, with no index configured to route it anywhere else (pypi/support#11895). ## What changed - `ci/install_pypi_proxy.sh` — the install, extracted so forge and manylinux share it instead of carrying two copies of the same twenty lines. The next image that needs it adds one `RUN`. - `ci/docker/manylinux-retag.Dockerfile` — installs the proxy and the `profile.d` script. Steps run under `bash -elic`, so it is sourced there exactly as in forge; the probe, the mode selection and the fail-open path are unchanged. - The interpreter is **discovered, not named**: manylinux ships a set under `/opt/python`, so the Dockerfile picks the newest that satisfies the proxy's `>=3.11` requirement and fails loudly (listing what it found) if there is none. That keeps working when the base image's interpreter set moves. The image's default python is untouched and the venv stays in `/opt/pypiproxy`. - Both wanda specs gain the files in `srcs`, without which the bind mounts have nothing to mount. ## What this does not cover `docker build` — the `wanda: wheel py3.*` steps still fetch from PyPI directly, because BuildKit `RUN` steps do not inherit the step container's environment. Those five fetches per build are pip's *isolated build environment* (`setuptools`, `cython`, `wheel`, `pip`, `packaging`), unpinned because `python/` has no `pyproject.toml`. Two follow-ups are possible there and neither belongs in this PR: passing the index as a build arg, which needs a stable address so wanda's content-addressed cache key does not churn per job, or `--no-build-isolation`, which removes those fetches outright. ## Testing - `bash -n` on the installer and on the new `RUN` block; `pre-commit` (shellcheck, semgrep, whitespace) clean over every changed file. - Not verified locally: the image build itself, which needs the manylinux base and a wanda run. The interpreter discovery is written to fail loudly rather than silently skip, so a wrong assumption about `/opt/python` shows up as a failed image build with the directory listing attached, not as a silently unwired image. - The real check is a build on this branch: manylinux steps should log `pypi index: …` the way forge steps already do. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for this change.
